articles.title: 'Social supermarket' SE Kitchen to take over vacant Chatham shop
articles.summary: SE Kitchen will open a third shop, adding to the social enterprise's units in Ashford and Ramsgate.
articles.body:
A "social supermarket" offering low-cost food and support to escape financial hardship is to open at a third location in Kent.

SE Kitchen is due to open at the Pentagon Shopping Centre in Chatham in October, adding to branches in Ashford and Ramsgate .

The food shops, run by Social Enterprise Kent, redistribute surplus food and offer cut-price groceries.

The community interest company's chief executive, Rebecca Smith, said: "We pride ourselves on creating a supportive, inclusive space where people can access what they need today while building a more stable, sustainable future."

The Chatham shop will be open to all Medway residents with no referral or membership required, and will provide a community meeting space.

It will also offer "wrap-around support designed to address the root causes of financial hardship", according to Medway Council.

Teresa Murray, the council's deputy leader, said access to affordable and healthy food was "critically important" and a key factor in people's well-being.

"Being able to put this new community supermarket in the heart of Chatham... is fantastic and will undoubtedly support the wider work we are undertaking," she said.

articles.title: Witney designer wraps blanket heritage into fashion contest
articles.summary: Alexandra Burch takes her Cotswold Remnants collection to The Redress Design Award final in Hong Kong.
articles.body:
A young designer is highlighting local craftsmanship through her womenswear collection for an international fashion competition.

Alexandra Burch, 19, from Witney is among the eight finalists on the Redress Design Award , which challenges emerging designers to use certified textile waste for their creations.

Cotswold Remnants celebrates her hometown heritage of blanket making and is "entirely made from materials and offcuts salvaged from the Cotswold Woollen Weavers, a mill that sadly had to permanently close this year ".

She was flown out to Hong Kong on Sunday ahead of the grand final fashion show on 2 September.

She said she was "really excited" for her first visit to Asia, where she will face off with designers from all over the world.

"I know that some are from Austria, Germany, some are from Hong Kong and mainland China.

"We're all coming together, so I'm excited to meet everyone soon."

Alexandra said she would do fittings for the runway show models.

"I'm still very inspired by the 70s and the hippie movement but this collection ... was inspired by tweed jackets and traditional farmer wear in my local area, so I looked more locally this time."

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

Her four-look collection was made of faulty tweed blankets and loom offcuts from the now closed mill in Filkins.

"It's all made of local British wool, undyed and naturally dyed," Alexandra said.

The designer, who is also a fashion design student at Kingston University, believes that "waste is not inevitable, it's a design decision".

"You should focus on sustainability at the start of your design, not add it on at the end.

"I think that true sustainability lies in valuing what already exists and designing for durability, so looking at the future."

The non-profit association Global Fashion Agenda , which aims to accelerate net-positive action in the industry, has found that "every year, 92 million tonnes of textile waste is produced globally".

The United Nations Environment Programme says this is the equivalent of "a garbage truck full of clothing being incinerated or sent to a landfill every second".

"I think at the moment the fashion industry is way out of hand, it's way too fast-paced and I think fast fashion brands must be held accountable," Alexandra said.

People can support their favourite designers in the competition's People's Choice vote which is open until 08:00 BST on 31 August.

The final will be streamed live on The Redress Design Award website .

articles.title: 'Game changer' study seeks answers for heavy periods and endometriosis
articles.summary: It will the create world's largest menstrual fluid biobank to improve treatment of heavy periods.
articles.body:
A major new research project aiming to transform care for women with heavy periods is to create the world's largest menstrual fluid biobank.

The CycleTrack study hopes to improve understanding of heavy menstrual bleeding and related conditions such as endometriosis and fibroids, helping speed up diagnosis and treatment for millions of women.

Led by researchers from the universities of Bristol and Exeter, it will collect real-time health data and menstrual fluid samples from thousands of women across the UK.

Professor Gemma Sharp said the study was going to be "a real game changer" for menstrual health research and could cut waiting times for effective treatment.

As part of the study, researchers are working with women who have personal experience of heavy periods.

Maria Lewis, 34, from Weston-super-Mare, has lived with heavy menstrual bleeding since she first started menstruating and was diagnosed with endometriosis last year.

She has taken part in the Children of the 90s , external study since childhood and was keen to support the latest research.

Describing the impact of her condition, she said: "It's horrific. I'm in pain every day."

Although she cannot take part in the menstrual fluid collection because she takes hormonal contraception to manage her symptoms and no longer menstruates, she believes the research could help improve understanding of conditions affecting women.

She said: "Absolutely, it needs more of a platform and a louder voice."

Heavy menstrual bleeding, sometimes known as HMB, affects up to half of women worldwide and can have a significant impact on physical, emotional and social wellbeing.

Symptoms can include periods lasting more than seven days, the need to change sanitary protection every one to two hours, passing large blood clots and signs of iron deficiency such as fatigue and dizziness.

Researchers say menstrual health remains poorly understood despite being a key indicator of overall health, partly because of a lack of high-quality data.

Recent studies have suggested heavy periods can affect many aspects of daily life , external , including educational attainment and school attendance.

The study will recruit participants from two long-running birth cohort studies: Children of the 90s in south-west England and Born in Bradford in West Yorkshire.

Thousands of volunteers will use a specialist app and detailed questionnaires to record symptoms, sleep, mood, energy levels and overall wellbeing.

Participants will also provide menstrual fluid samples over three menstrual cycles using specially designed period pads.

By linking those samples with long-term health information and genetic data already held by the cohort studies, researchers hope to uncover biological signals associated with heavy menstrual bleeding.

They believe the findings could lead to earlier diagnosis, more personalised treatment plans and new methods of identifying health risks linked to heavy periods, including iron deficiency.

The project is being led by Sharp, an epidemiologist at the University of Exeter who specialises in women's health research.

She said: "HMB is excessive menstrual blood loss that interferes with your physical, social, emotional and/or quality of life.

"It can occur with or without underlying pathology such as fibroids, hormonal issues.

"Common symptoms can often include: bleeding lasting longer than seven days, needing to change protection every one to two hours, passing large clots, signs of iron deficiency anaemia (e.g. fatigue, dizziness)."

The study is part of a wider international programme known as The Missed Vital Sign, , external led by Wellcome Leap, which aims to dramatically reduce the time women wait for effective treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding.

Professor Sharp said CycleTrack would be the largest bank of dried menstrual fluid samples in the world.

She added: "We'll be able to understand what causes different conditions, like endometriosis, fibroids, the impact of those conditions on other areas of life, and then hopefully new ways to predict, prevent, and treat those symptoms as well."

Researchers say the work could help address long-standing gaps in understanding menstrual health and improve support for millions of women.

Although periods are experienced by around half the population during their lifetime, campaigners and health experts have often argued menstrual health has not received the same level of research attention as many other areas of medicine.

The CycleTrack , external team hopes the large volume of data generated by the study will provide new insights into how heavy periods affect everyday life, work, education and general health.

The information could also help shape future guidance for schools and employers on supporting people affected by heavy menstrual bleeding.

Scientists say many women face delays in diagnosis and treatment, while some may not realise symptoms such as extreme tiredness or dizziness can be linked to blood loss and iron deficiency.

By analysing biological samples alongside day-to-day symptom information, the team hopes to identify markers that could eventually help clinicians recognise problems sooner and tailor treatment more effectively.

Sample collection is due to begin this month, with researchers expecting data from thousands of participants to contribute to what they describe as a step change in understanding menstrual health.

All the data will have been collected by end of November 2027. Preliminary findings will follow by early 2028.

Currently only Children of the 90s and Born in Bradford participants can take part, but the research team has a waiting list , external if people are interested in taking part in future studies (funding dependent).

articles.title: Lunar Eclipse on Raksha Bandhan 2026: Will sutak affect Rakhi Rituals? Can you tie rakhi normally in India?
articles.summary: Rituals & Puja News: Raksha Bandhan 2026 comes with an unusual celestial coincidence. On August 28, the same day as Raksha Bandhan, a deep partial lunar eclipse will take .
articles.body: Raksha Bandhan 2026 comes with an unusual celestial coincidence. On August 28, the same day as Raksha Bandhan, a deep partial lunar eclipse will take place. At its peak, more than 90% of the Moon will enter Earthâs umbral shadow.Naturally, this has created one big question:Should you change your Rakhi rituals because of Chandra Grahan?For people celebrating Raksha Bandhan in India, the short answer is: No, not simply because an eclipse is happening somewhere on Earth.The Most Important Detail: The Eclipse Is Not Visible in IndiaThis is where much of the confusion begins.The lunar eclipse takes place on August 28, but it will not be visible from India. During the eclipse, the Moon will already be below the horizon here.This distinction is important from a traditional perspective as well.In many commonly followed Dharmic traditions, Grahan-related observances and Sutak are associated with the visibility of the eclipse at a particular location. Therefore, if you are celebrating Raksha Bandhan in India, you do not need to automatically observe eclipse-related Sutak merely because the astronomical eclipse falls on the same date.So, Can You Tie Rakhi Normally in India?Yes.If you are in India, the eclipse itself does not require you to cancel Raksha Bandhan, postpone Rakhi, stop the puja, or treat the entire day as inauspicious.Your Rakhi timing should instead be decided according to Purnima Tithi, Bhadra, local sunrise, and the appropriate Raksha Bandhan Muhurta, as you would normally do.This is an important distinction:An eclipse existing astronomically and an eclipse being ritually applicable at your location are not necessarily the same thing.So, don't allow a social-media headline saying âChandra Grahan on Raksha Bandhanâ to create unnecessary fear.Does the Eclipse Still Have Astrological Significance?This is where we need to separate ritual rules from astrological interpretation.The planetary alignment of August 28 places the Moon in Aquarius, while Rahu is also positioned in Aquarius. On the opposite side, the Sun, Mercury, and Ketu strongly activate Leo, while Jupiter remains exalted in Cancer.So, astrologically, this is certainly an interesting Raksha Bandhan.The larger theme is not fear. It is about relationships, emotional patterns, family roots, individuality, and protection.Rakhi itself is a festival built around Rakshaâthe conscious promise of protection. So, instead of becoming anxious about Grahan, use the occasion to look at the sibling relationship beyond photographs, sweets, and gifts.Has distance quietly entered the relationship?Is there something unresolved between you?Are you protecting your sibling, or sometimes trying to control them?Is an old family disagreement still being carried unnecessarily?Those questions are far more useful than becoming frightened simply because the word Grahan appears on the calendar.Get the latest religion news and spiritual insights. articles.title: RSPB reports record-breaking Cornish chough numbers
articles.summary: RSPB England says 161 Choughs have been counted - 32 more than the 129 recorded last year.
articles.body:
A record-breaking number of choughs have made their nests around the Cornish coastline this summer proving the breed is in "robust health", a bird conservation charity has said.

RSPB England said 161 choughs had been counted in Cornwall - 32 more than the 129 recorded in 2025 .

The charity said the new birds came from 56 successful breeding pairs meaning the average productivity of a Cornish chough nest was three fledglings.

It said choughs died out in Cornwall in the 1970s but returned in 2001 when three birds believed to be from Ireland landed at Lizard Point and began the rebreeding of the population.

Peter Hall, a National Trust chough monitoring volunteer on the Lizard, is on his 11th year of monitoring the nest sites.

He said he had not foreseen a time when he would be monitoring so many sites and "certainly not having 16 choughlets fledge".

Hall said: "The past two winters we have been blessed with chatterings in excess of 20 chough around the Lizard - a far cry from the solitary single pair we had when I started as part of the then nest protection team in 2016.

"Long may the successful return of this iconic Cornish bird delight myself and others."

The charity said the Lizard was the prime breeding ground for the Cornish chough with 26 chicks, 11 more than 2025, emerging from eight nests on the peninsula.

National Trust volunteer Lydia Allt said 2026 had been "an exceptional one" for choughs on the Lizard and across Cornwall.

She said: "Thanks to a quarter of a century of conservation work, partnership working and the support of local farmers and land managers, we are seeing record numbers ofchough across the area.

"Their remarkable recovery shows what can be achieved when habitats are restored and protected, giving wildlife the space it needs to thrive.

"To see so many choughs successfully breeding and feeding across the Lizard is incredibly encouraging and highlights the importance of continuing to care for this special landscape for future generations."

Andrew Jones, chough conservation officer for the RSPB in Cornwall, said the repopulation work would not be possible without volunteers.

He said: "There has been a huge volunteer effort over the past 25 years to protect and monitor Cornwall's iconic choughs and we're grateful to everyone who has played their part in this conservation success story.

"This year, the RSPB and National Trust have had a team of around 50 dedicated volunteer chough watchers, covering the coastline from the Roseland all the way round to Bude, monitoring the breeding efforts and reporting back so we could collate these fantastic, record-breaking numbers."

articles.title: Chloe Moffat: Dad of woman who took her own life says Treasury failed in its duty of care
articles.summary: Chloe Moffat died last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.
articles.body:
The father of a civil service employee who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers has said the lack of support given to her by the Treasury "beggars belief".

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, David Moffat said he did not feel the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death.

He added that her loss was "devastating", and had "torn such a big hole in our lives".

The Treasury said "it will learn the lessons from this tragedy".

On 19 May 2025, Chloe went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

"Chloe's first comment was, 'Oh, this must be serious, there's two of you here'", David told Today's Emma Barnett. "So that's the first time that she was aware of anything [that] might be a to do."

"And then they worked through and put several allegations to her that she'd shared confidential information."

During the meeting, David said she had asked on several occasions if she would lose her job, and if she could have a friend there - both of which were refused.

A coroner found at an inquest earlier in August that the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy, which would have made clear that if the allegations against Chloe were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

"Even though she asked, they said they could not determine the outcome," David said.

Straight after the meeting, Chloe was locked out of her emails. "That was all part of the shock and awe of it all for Chloe," David said.

The coroner found that the meeting between Chloe and her managers "materially contributed" to her death.

Treasury contributed to woman's death, inquest hears Published 10 August

Treasury contributed to woman's death, inquest hears

David said that "there wasn't any duty of care" shown to Chloe by the Treasury.

"There was no safeguarding, there was no support during or after that meeting, from what we've seen and what we've read", he said.

"It beggars belief that an organisation that is front and central in our government cannot get it right."

Asked whether he felt the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death, he answered: "Not yet".

He added, however, that he and his wife had received a letter on Tuesday from the Treasury's permanent secretary, James Bowler, and that they had also met him last August.

David said while they could not change what happened to Chloe, he wanted "to ensure" that "lessons are learned".

"If something positive can come from this unbearable loss that we're suffering, that's all we look to achieve."

He said he and his wife Anne were unsure if they would be pursuing further action against the Treasury, but that they wanted "redress".

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The Treasury's deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe's friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague.

"We will learn the lessons from this tragedy. We are working urgently to respond to the coroner's findings and we have introduced immediate changes to our guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements.

"Chloe's parents have agreed to meet with us so we can hear their views and update on actions the department is taking."

articles.title: Chloe Moffat: Dad of woman who took her own life says Treasury failed in its duty of care
articles.summary: Chloe Moffat died last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.
articles.body:
The father of a civil service employee who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers has said the lack of support given to her by the Treasury "beggars belief".

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, David Moffat said he did not feel the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death.

He added that her loss was "devastating", and had "torn such a big hole in our lives".

The Treasury said "it will learn the lessons from this tragedy".

On 19 May 2025, Chloe went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

"Chloe's first comment was, 'Oh, this must be serious, there's two of you here'", David told Today's Emma Barnett. "So that's the first time that she was aware of anything [that] might be a to do."

"And then they worked through and put several allegations to her that she'd shared confidential information."

During the meeting, David said she had asked on several occasions if she would lose her job, and if she could have a friend there - both of which were refused.

A coroner found at an inquest earlier in August that the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy, which would have made clear that if the allegations against Chloe were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

"Even though she asked, they said they could not determine the outcome," David said.

Straight after the meeting, Chloe was locked out of her emails. "That was all part of the shock and awe of it all for Chloe," David said.

The coroner found that the meeting between Chloe and her managers "materially contributed" to her death.

Treasury contributed to woman's death, inquest hears

David said that "there wasn't any duty of care" shown to Chloe by the Treasury.

"There was no safeguarding, there was no support during or after that meeting, from what we've seen and what we've read", he said.

"It beggars belief that an organisation that is front and central in our government cannot get it right."

Asked whether he felt the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death, he answered: "Not yet".

He added, however, that he and his wife had received a letter on Tuesday from the Treasury's permanent secretary, James Bowler, and that they had also met him last August.

David said while they could not change what happened to Chloe, he wanted "to ensure" that "lessons are learned".

"If something positive can come from this unbearable loss that we're suffering, that's all we look to achieve."

He said he and his wife Anne were unsure if they would be pursuing further action against the Treasury, but that they wanted "redress".

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The Treasury's deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe's friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague.

"We will learn the lessons from this tragedy. We are working urgently to respond to the coroner's findings and we have introduced immediate changes to our guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements.

articles.title: AI receptionist could not understand me, says Doncaster stroke patient
articles.summary: Judith Butterfield from Doncaster says she could not get past the AI service EMMA.
articles.body:
A woman recovering from a stroke has said she was "upset and frustrated" that an AI reception service at her GP surgery could not understand her, prompting her to register elsewhere.

The ASA surgery at Armthorpe near Doncaster was one of many facilities using a nationwide AI system called EMMA to prevent long wait times on the phone.

Judith Butterfield, 71, said after her stroke she attempted to book a GP appointment five times but could not get past the AI service.

Practice manager Claire Oxley said the EMMA service had been "decommissioned" at Armthorpe and was no longer used at the surgery.

Butterfield originally spent two months at Doncaster Royal Infirmary following a stroke in January.

It primarily affected the strength and mobility down the right side of her body and left her speech fragmented.

The grandmother said that the issues with EMMA were compounded because the AI service asked patients not to use speakerphone.

Butterfield said: "I need to hold the phone in my left hand but I can't use the keypad now with my right hand so what am I supposed to do?

"It's not appropriate as a service to have a robot taking details.

"It should be a more personal thing where you're talking to a person and asking questions.

"There was a point in the conversation where I had to repeat my name and she just couldn't understand me.

"If it's a person they can say, 'could you spell that?' But the call just dropped off. It was very difficult and upsetting."

After growing frustrated with the AI service at Armthorpe, the former HR worker has now registered with the Burns Practice in Doncaster.

"They have very good, friendly, helpful receptionists," she said.

"There's still the wait when you phone up and you're in a queue but you can use a call-back service.

"I was amazed when I spoke to a person."

According to the watchdog Healthwatch, Butterfield's experience is not unique with other Yorkshire patients struggling to be understood by AI reception services.

Oxley said: "I am sorry to hear this patient encountered difficulties and felt the need to move to another surgery.

"I can confirm the AI EMMA service has been decommissioned and the practice are no longer using this system.

"We would welcome the patient back to the surgery and I can assure this lady and others that we have successfully recruited more reception staff to help improve our service to patients."

A spokesperson for QuantumLoopAI, the company behind the system, said: "We are sorry to hear about this patient's experience.

"Nobody should feel they have to change practice to be heard, and with her consent we would welcome the chance to look into what happened and help put it right."

The company said every practice using EMMA could set up "priority routing", allowing patients to go "straight through to the reception team on every call".

articles.title: How drought is changing nature's calendar in the West
articles.summary: From early berries to falling leaves, drought is making parts of the West look like autumn.
articles.body:
Trees shedding leaves, berries ripening weeks early and brown landscapes are giving parts of the West an autumn-like appearance despite it still being August.

Experts warn record-breaking temperatures and prolonged dry weather are having wide-ranging impacts on nature, from wildlife food supplies to the health of the soil beneath our feet.

Wildlife conservationist Steve England said: "Trees should be full of leaf. Instead, they look how they should in November, but we're only in August."

Professor Mark Everard, from the University of the West of England (UWE), said while there are "winners and losers" in nature, it is important to see it as "a highly integrated machine that's breaking down".

Heavy periods study to create world's largest biobank

Supercars seized ahead of wedding after M5 incident

Autistic DJ befriended at festival given 'dream' set

England, who has lived near Stoke Park in Bristol all his life, has also noticed fruit ripening much earlier than normal.

He remembers picking blackberries as a child at the end of the school holidays in August and September, but this year he was out picking in June.

However, some berries are also suffering in the drought. England said rowan berries should be double their current size by now, but many have shrivelled in the dry conditions.

He fears that could have consequences for migratory birds such as fieldfares and redwings, which rely on autumn berries as a food source when they arrive in the UK for winter.

If they're "ripening too quick" and disappearing before the birds arrive it could be a "big problem", he said.

He has also noticed trees dropping their leaves much earlier than usual due to the dry weather.

"They are going into survival mode," he added.

Everard described the heat as a "trend that's getting progressively worse" and compared the landscape of Wiltshire, where he lives, to India and Africa with its "Savannah colours".

But he said the "bigger problem" is what lies under the soil.

During intensively dry and hot periods, activity below ground "basically shuts down" and also soil begins to lose structure, which has "major ramifications for everything we can see above the surface" now and in years to come, added Everard, who is associate professor of ecosystem services at UWE.

Although nature has amazing resilience and is able to adapt to a range of extremes, Everard said the problem is "we've changed those extremes".

Record temperatures and record low rainfall can "break nature's capacities to respond" and the system begins to "disintegrate".

Everard said "nature gives us clues and we should be wise enough to listen to those clues".

Paul Keene, who runs a pick-your-own strawberry farm near Cheltenham in Gloucestershire, has also seen crops ripen much earlier than expected.

He said they normally start picking outside in mid to late June, but this year had their first pick in May, which is "incredibly early and all driven by the heat".

The dry weather has not caused major problems for the farm because it has its own reservoir, which collects water and feeds an automated watering system for the fruit.

At the height of the summer temperatures, strawberries were being watered up to 12 times a day.

It is not just strawberries that have ripened sooner than expected, pumpkins on the farm are already looking Halloween-ready.

In previous years, Keene said they have been "waiting for them to ripen in October" so this is very early and may mean they have to be brought in for storage to make sure they last.

articles.title: At least 15 newborns die in Pakistan hospital fire
articles.summary: At least 15 newborn babies died in a fire at a maternity ward in Pakistan's capital Islamabad, local rescue officials told dpa on Wednesday. The fire was lik...
articles.body:
At least 15 newborn babies died in a fire at a maternity ward in Pakistan's capital Islamabad, local rescue officials told dpa on Wednesday.

The fire was likely caused by a malfunctioning air conditioning unit in the early hours of the morning, the officials said.

Only one of the newborns in the ward was rescued, they said. The fire was now under control.

The maternity ward is part of the gynaecology department at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), a state-run hospital. At least 16 newborns were in the nursery when the fire broke out.

Television footage from Geo News showed heavy smoke and firefighters working at the scene. The broadcaster said an investigation would be launched into the further causes of the fire.

Public hospitals in Pakistan are unpopular because of lower standards, with those who can afford it opting for private clinics for better care. Lax safety standards have repeatedly led to tragedies in Pakistan.

articles.title: Channel Islands on course for 'hottest ever summer'
articles.summary: Guernsey and Jersey are set to have seen the warmest summer ever, says the Met Office.
articles.body:
The summer of 2026 is on course to be the Channel Islands' hottest since records began, according to local meteorologists.

Provisional statistics from Jersey Met show Jersey's average temperature, measured across both day and night, was 20.9C (69.6F) between 1 June and 15 August. That is 3.2C (5.8F) above the 1991 to 2020 average.

Guernsey's mean temperature over the same period, and with two weeks of summer to go, is 19.2°C (66.56F), some 3C (5.4F) above the average, meteorologists said.

It was in line with evidence that climate change was driving hotter summers and increasing the likelihood of drier conditions, they added.

There have also been record-breaking temperatures across the islands, with Guernsey reaching 36.4°C (97.52F) on 25 June, its highest temperature ever recorded; and Jersey reaching 39.3°C (102.74F) on the same day, also its highest temperature on record.

Alongside the summer heat, the islands have experienced significantly lower than average rainfall.

In Jersey, 69.6mm of rain fell over the summer, compared with a 30-year average of 158.0mm.

In Guernsey, 43.2mm of rain was recorded, well below the 30-year average of 147.6mm.

Unlike large parts of the UK, this lack of rain has not led to drought conditions or hosepipe band across the islands.

Paul Aked, from Jersey Met, said the summer had not been too dissimilar to famous drought of 1976 , although 2026 had actually been hotter, with more heatwave periods and higher peak temperatures.

Aked went on to say, in terms of the heat and how people felt it: "It is very different for the islands when we're comparing ourselves with a city in the United Kingdom.

"We have the sea around us, which is cooler than the air temperature, and that does influence [where we] get some cooling from."

He added: "Just because we've had a hot summer, it doesn't mean we're going to get a particularly cold or wet or wintry winter."

articles.title: Solihull mum's perforated bowel ordeal after scan error
articles.summary: Mum developed sepsis after scan error and now calls for better postnatal care for women.
articles.body:
"No-one should have to go through what I did after having a baby," said Natalie after a harrowing post-birth ordeal.

On 11 January 2023, she welcomed her baby girl into the world by caesarean section at Birmingham's Good Hope Hospital, but the newborn bliss soon turned sour and she was left needing emergency surgery for a perforated bowel.

"I knew something wasn't right after Brooke was born, but it felt like my concerns weren't being taken seriously," the 37-year-old from Solihull said.

A University Hospitals Birmingham spokesperson said the Trust "is committed to providing safe, high-quality care" to all patients and to "learning from when things do not go as expected."

Just days after the birth, she began to suffer severe pain and swelling in her abdomen but says her symptoms were downplayed.

As well as debilitating pain, she also suffered vomiting, which included faecal matter, but on 14 January, doctors misinterpreted her scan as showing temporary slowing of her bowel's movements following surgery, medical negligence lawyers at Irwin Mitchell said.

"My condition got worse over several days. Being told I needed emergency surgery is something I'll never forget. I was frightened I might die," the factory worker added.

Despite raising concerns, her condition deteriorated and she developed sepsis. On 18 January, she underwent emergency surgery, in which part of her bowel was removed and a stoma fitted.

The Trust admitted admitted a breach of duty and that a CT scan carried out four days earlier was incorrectly reported.

Decisions about Natalie's care were based on that error, the Trust has said.

"As legal discussions are ongoing, it would not be appropriate to comment on the detail of the case, however, we are working constructively with [Natalie's] representatives."

The mother, who also has a 15-year-old son, explained: "The impact on my life has been huge and I still live with the effects. I continue to struggle with pain, fatigue and digestive problems. It's affected everything from being able to do daily tasks to how I've been able to care for Brooke and Callum."

Natalie is now campaigning for women to receive better care following childbirth and to ensure their concerns are heard.

She added: "I just want other women to be listened to and for warning signs after birth not to be missed."

Jade Elliott-Archer, of Irwin Mitchell, said: "Our investigations have identified concerning failings in how Natalie's condition was recognised and responded to as her condition worsened.

"While these admissions provide Natalie with answers she deserves, they also highlight serious concerns about the care women can receive after birth."

Natalie has since had further surgery, including reversal of the stoma and treatment for complications including a hernia and ongoing wound problems.

"If my experience helps improve care for even one mum, then it will have been worth it," she said.

articles.title: 'Very close call' as fire nearly hits Jersey Water plant
articles.summary: Firefighters tackle flames which were near to Jersey Water's desalination plant in Corbiere.
articles.body:
A large fire came "dangerously close" to a desalination plant, water bosses have said.

Jersey Water said the incident which was tackled by the island's firefighters in a nearby field in Corbiere on Monday highlighted the stark risks posed by wildfires in the current dry conditions.

It said if the plant, which turns sea water into drinking water, had been damaged, Jersey would have lost "critical resilience" to the island's water supply during prolonged periods of dry weather.

The utility company said it was "extremely grateful" to Jersey Fire Service, its own staff and the public for acting quickly to protect the plant.

Jersey Fire Service said 18 firefighters went to the scene after a bonfire lit in a dry field was spread by strong winds.

It issued a warning against people lighting fires in the open as conditions across the island remained "very dry".

Jersey Water echoed the fire service's warning and said people should take extra care and avoid activities which could start a fire.

"This incident was certainly a very close call and a stark reminder of the risks posed by wildfire," a company spokesperson said.

"The desalination plant is a vital part of Jersey's drought response.

"Had it been damaged, we would have lost critical resilience for the island's water supply during prolonged dry periods."

articles.title: PSNI officer sacked after investigation finds 'catalogue of corruption'
articles.summary: A Police Ombudsman investigation found the constable failed to disclose multiple conflicts of interest, intimidated a former partner, attempted to falsify evidence and asked a colleague to lie.
articles.body:
A Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) officer has been dismissed after an investigation found he initiated a sexual relationship with a woman he met in the course of his duties.

A Police Ombudsman inquiry also found he failed to disclose multiple conflicts of interest, intimidated a former partner, attempted to falsify evidence and asked a colleague to lie.

Ombudsman Jacqui Durkin said the behaviour was a "catalogue of corruption" which had "the potential to do serious damage to public trust and confidence in policing".

The PSNI said the officer's behaviour was "unacceptable and clearly falls far below the standards the public rightly expects at all times from police officers and staff".

Durkin said the officer, known in the investigation as Police Officer B, was a constable "of some experience" and that the allegations he faced was "one of the most serious types of police corruption".

She added that there was "no place for him, or any other officer, in the PSNI who misconducts himself in this way".

"This should send out a clear message to any other officers who may be involved in that type of behaviour that the consequences are that you will be dismissed."

Abuse of position for sexual purposes (APSP) cases currently account for 36% of the most serious cases currently under investigation by the Police Ombudsman's Office.

Investigators at the Police Ombudsman's office spent almost two years working through, what Durkin described as a "very complex, multi-stranded investigation".

Following the completion of the Police Ombudsman's investigation, a file was submitted to the Public Prosecution Service who issued a no prosecution decision in October 2024.

The case stemmed from an assault allegation made to the police by one woman, Woman A, against another, Woman B, who then made a counter assault allegation, in 2018.

The police officer responsible for investigating the incident, Police Officer A, asked a colleague, Police Officer B, to take a statement from Woman B.

Police Officer B, did not disclose that he had been in a sexual relationship with Woman A in 2016 and was still in contact with her socially.

Within 24 hours of meeting Woman B to take her statement, he had contacted her through Facebook and Snapchat and then began a sexual relationship with her.

A short time later they were living together and had a child before their relationship ended in early 2020.

The investigation also extended to a further incident in 2021 when another woman who had been in a relationship with Police Officer B reported that she had received a threatening, anonymous letter.

The letter was sent a short time after Police Officer B had been made aware that he was being investigated for his contact with vulnerable women.

It included an intimate photograph of the woman and also made threats that more photos would be sent to her family.

The only person she had shared the photo with was her former boyfriend, Police Officer B.

Two weeks before she received the letter, she had also received a phone notification that he had downloaded all the images she had shared.

When examined, the police officer's phone contained 51 images of the woman including intimate photos similar to the one she had received anonymously through the post.

The PSNI held a misconduct hearing in April and the officer was dismissed without notice.

The panel found that the officer had misconducted himself by breaching the PSNI Code of Ethics.

Police Officer B was the seventh officer to be dismissed as a result of Police Ombudsman investigations in APSP since 2020.

A further police officer received a written final warning.

In Northern Ireland, there is no specific 'misconduct in public office' offence. It is, instead, a common law offence.

Durkin hopes that the new Public Office (Accountability) Bill that is going through parliament will create a specific misconduct in public office offence.

She also welcomed the development of the Justice Bill that is making its way through the Northern Ireland Assembly.

"[This will] fast track some of those cases so that we would no longer have to wait until the conclusion of a decision to prosecute," she said.

This way, she explained, where there is "clear evidence of misconduct", the police can decide whether they dismiss an officer based on the evidence-led ombudsman investigation.

"Where you have predatory police officers, it's important that victims or complainants... can be assured of evidence led, impartial and independent investigation".

Chief Superintendent Stephen Murray, Head of the PSNI's professional standards department, said the serious misconduct identified in this case was "unacceptable and clearly falls far below the standards the public rightly expects, at all times, from police officers and staff".

"Police officers are entrusted with significant powers and responsibilities. That trust must never be abused for personal or sexual gain.

"Abuse of position for sexual purposes is wholly unacceptable, it is a serious abuse of authority and a breach of the trust placed in policing by the public.

"The behaviour found in this case was simply intolerable. It involved failures to declare conflicts of interest, dishonesty and conduct which undermined the integrity, impartiality and professionalism expected of every police officer."

The dismissal without notice, he added, reflected how serious the organisation took these matters "and reinforces our position that there is no place for corruption or abuse of position for sexual purposes in policing".

articles.title: An Oregon high-school junior remembered feeling lost during her first research internship, so she built a free student-led platform to help other teens find mentors and publish research
articles.summary: US News: For many high-school students, becoming interested in research is easier than figuring out how to actually begin. Finding a mentor, understanding rese.
articles.body: For many high-school students, becoming interested in research is easier than figuring out how to actually begin. Finding a mentor, understanding research methods, and knowing how to publish or share completed work can be difficult without the right guidance. Riya Velhal, an Oregon high-school junior, experienced that uncertainty herself during her first research internship. Instead of allowing that experience to discourage her, she used it as inspiration to create a student-led initiative aimed at helping other students navigate research with greater confidence.According to Velhal's profile on StratScholar, she began her first internship at the start of her sophomore year and remembers feeling âextremely lost.â Her experience eventually inspired her to create StratScholar, a student-led initiative focused on giving young researchers access to mentorship, resources, and opportunities to share their work.A difficult first experienceVelhal's introduction to research did not come with a clear roadmap. During her first internship, she found herself without the resources, support system and community needed to understand how research worked. For a high-school student, that can make an already complicated process feel overwhelming. Research involves more than choosing an interesting topic. Students need to learn how to develop questions, find reliable information, understand existing research and communicate their findings. Without someone to provide direction, it can be difficult to know whether an idea is worth pursuing or what steps should come next.Velhal's own experience made her recognise that the problem could potentially affect other students as well. There could be many students interested in research who simply lacked someone to guide them. That realisation became the starting point for StratScholar.Turning experience into actionRather than viewing her difficult first internship as a setback, Velhal used it to think about how the research experience could be made easier for other teenagers. Her answer was to create a student-led platform where young people could find research opportunities, connect with mentors and develop their research interests.StratScholar is built around the idea that students should not have to rely entirely on existing personal connections to discover research opportunities. The organisation aims to make research experiences more accessible to middle and high-school students. The initiative also emphasises students learning from one another. Instead of presenting research as something available only to students who already understand the academic system, StratScholar seeks to create a community where young researchers can receive guidance while developing their own interests. For Velhal, this mission is closely connected to her own development as a researcher.Her journey into researchAfter her first internship, Velhal continued exploring research independently. Her StratScholar profile notes that she became involved in independent research related to campaign finance, giving her an opportunity to explore a subject in greater depth. That progression is significant because her experience moved from uncertainty to independent exploration. The student who initially felt lost while trying to understand research eventually began working on her own research interests and thinking about how other students could receive better support.It also appears to have shaped the way she views mentorship. Having experienced the difficulty of entering research without enough guidance, Velhal's work with StratScholar focuses on making that initial transition easier for others.A platform for young researchersStratScholar is not simply intended to connect students with research projects. Its broader purpose is to help teenagers develop the skills and confidence needed to participate in research. The organisation provides opportunities intended to help students learn about research while connecting them with mentors and other students. Its focus extends beyond the research process itself, encouraging students to develop communication, presentation and leadership skills alongside their academic work.This matters because completing a research project is only one part of the experience. Students also need to know how to explain their findings and communicate their ideas effectively. For teenagers interested in eventually pursuing academic careers, those skills can be valuable.Making research less intimidatingKnowing where to begin can be one of the biggest challenges for young researchers. A student might have an interesting question but have no idea which expert to contact. Another might complete a project but not know how to present or publish it. Someone else might simply need another student to explain how the research process works.StratScholar is intended to address those early obstacles by bringing resources and mentorship together in one student-focused initiative. The emphasis on accessibility is also important. Research opportunities can sometimes feel out of reach for students who do not already have connections to universities, researchers, or specialised programmes. A platform built specifically for younger students can provide a more approachable entry point.From feeling lost to helping othersVelhal's story ultimately began with a problem she personally encountered. She entered her first research internship excited about the opportunity but found herself unsure about what to do next. Instead of keeping that experience to herself, she turned it into a question: how could other students avoid feeling the same way?That question eventually became StratScholar. Her work demonstrates how a frustrating experience can sometimes lead to a practical solution. By creating a student-led initiative focused on mentorship, research opportunities, and sharing student work, Velhal is attempting to make the research journey more accessible to teenagers who might otherwise struggle to find their way.For young students interested in research, having an idea is often only the beginning. Finding someone who can help turn that idea into meaningful work can make all the difference. StratScholar is Velhal's effort to make that connection easier, and to ensure that fewer students have to feel as lost as she once did.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: SpaceXâs $100 billion bet on Louisiana Starbase: 3,000 jobs, rocket hub - why it matters
articles.summary: US News: SpaceX plans to build a $100 billion, 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) Starship launch complex on Pecan Island in US' southern Louisiana, an area that se.
articles.body: SpaceX plans to build a $100 billion, 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) Starship launch complex on Pecan Island in US' southern Louisiana, an area that serves as protected habitat for dozens of migratory bird species and whose receding wetlands help shield inland communities from flooding.The proposed Starbase Louisiana would become SpaceX's fourth US launch site and its second Starbase. Construction is due to begin in 2027, with the first Starship launch targeted for 2029 and thousands of missions annually envisioned over time.SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell presented the plans near the proposed site in Vermilion Parish alongside Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry and other senior state officials, according to Reuters.Exxon settlement cleared way for launch plansSpaceX's arrival follows the end of a roughly decade-long legal battle over wetland loss involving the same coastal area.Local parishes had sued ExxonMobil, alleging that coastal drilling and canal dredging by the oil company contributed to the disappearance of Louisiana wetlands. The state and Exxon agreed to settle the case in June, and a court order shows it was dismissed the following month.The resolution cleared the way for SpaceX's proposed development along an approximately 18-mile (29-km) coastal strip. Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois said discussions between the company and the state had been under way since February.Shotwell said extensive parts of the site would remain natural wetland without buildings or other infrastructure. An animated presentation released by SpaceX showed several launch pads separated by large green areas.Site would make fuel and generate powerSpaceX planned the Louisiana facility as a largely self-sustaining launch base rather than a rocket factory.The complex is expected to produce methane for Starship propellant, generate its own electricity and include vehicle-processing facilities. Deep-water shipping infrastructure would allow Starships to be transported from Texas, while Shotwell said the site would probably also have an airport.Unlike SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas, rockets would not be manufactured at this complex.Pecan Island's location also serves SpaceX's satellite plans. Launches heading south across Gulf waters could reach sun-synchronous orbits, whose sunlight conditions are suitable for the solar-powered AI satellites envisioned by Elon Musk.SpaceX targets thousands of Starship missionsThe company eventually wants Starbase Louisiana to handle thousands of Starship missions a year, although reaching that frequency will depend on SpaceX overcoming technical and regulatory obstacles.Starship remains under development. Landry has backed the project as a source of employment, investment and coastal protection.The development is part of a broader expansion by SpaceX across the southern United States. articles.title: At least 15 infants are killed in Islamabad hospital fire, local media reports
articles.summary: At least 15 infants were killed when a fire broke out at a state-run hospital in Pakistan‘s capital Islamabad, triggered by a fault in air conditioning systems, local broadcaster Geo TV reported on Wednesday.
articles.body: ISLAMABAD — At least 15 infants were killed when a fire broke out at a state-run hospital in Pakistan’s capital, Islamabad, set off by a fault in air-conditioning systems, local broadcaster Geo TV reported Wednesday. The blaze started around 7 a.m. (10 p.m. Tuesday ET) at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), on the third floor of the hospital’s mother and child health ward, the broadcaster said. The incident is among the deadliest hospital fires in recent years in the country, where government health care is subsidized but facilities are under-resourced and overburdened while watchdogs have frequently criticized state-run facilities as mismanaged. There were 16 newborns in the ward when the fire broke out, one of whom was rescued, Geo reported. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has directed authorities to conduct an immediate investigation, his office said. “Those responsible should be identified, and the strictest action should be taken,” Sharif’s office said in a statement. The ward was cordoned off and ambulances were seen outside the hospital building, according to a Reuters witness. PIMS, centrally located in Islamabad, is one of the city’s main public hospitals. Jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan was briefly treated there last week.

articles.title: Your guide to Shrewsbury Folk Festival
articles.summary: The festival takes place from Friday to Monday at the West Midlands Showground in Shrewsbury.
articles.body:
One of the biggest events in the folk music calendar is returning to Shropshire.

Shrewsbury Folk Festival is held at the West Midlands Showground from 28 to 31 August.

Thousands are expected to attend, with musical acts, dancing, workshops and a youth festival on the schedule.

Here is everything to expect from the four-day event.

Gates open for Thursday camping ticket holders from 15:00 to 18:00 BST.

For Friday camping, they open from 07:00.

Day ticket holders can get in from 12:00 on Friday and 09:00 on Saturday, Sunday and Monday.

Attendees should already have received e-tickets.

The festival starts at 15:00 on Friday, finishing at about 00:00.

On Saturday and Sunday, it begins at 12:00 and finishes at 00:45, while on Monday, things kick off at 12:00 and finishes at 18:00.

West Midlands Showground, Berwick Road, Shrewsbury, SY1 2PF

Yes - there is a car park field on site.

Campers get a free car park pass on arrival, while parking for non-campers can be either booked online or paid for by cash or card on the day.

Car parking is available from 12:00 on Friday and is manned by volunteers in the day and patrolled by security at night.

National Express runs coaches into Shrewsbury.

You can also get a bus to and from the site into Shrewsbury on Saturday and Sunday.

They leave the festival site at gate 1 every 15 minutes and will run between 09:00 and 18:00, with the final bus arriving back at the showground at 18:05.

Shrewsbury train station is a 10-15 minute walk away from the showground.

There are no specific areas where you can leave bicycles.

One side of the festival perimeter is a chainlink fence which bicycles can be chained to.

There are five main stages/areas across the four days: Severn, Pengwern, Sabrina, Village and Dance Tent.

Musical acts include names like Andy Fairweather Low & The Low Riders; Fantastic Negrito; Cara Dillon; Dustbowl Revival; and Talisk x Gardener Brothers: Unleashed.

Barbecues are allowed as long as they are constructed properly and are at least 18 inches (45.7cm) off the ground.

Open fires on the grass and disposable barbecues are not allowed.

Organisers say a bucket of water or sand should be kept nearby in case of an emergency.

They should be situated away from tents and caravans and should not be left unattended.

"We are constantly reviewing the situation in light of the weather and recent wildfires and may revise our guidance," organisers said on the event website.

"Look out for updates via email and social media and for signs on site."

Pandemonium! festival for children aged from birth to 11. Includes music, dance, crafts, storytelling, drama in a dedicated zone in the main arena

Refolkus - a space for 11 to 20-year-olds to music, dance, learn circus skills, henna tattooing and more. Located in The Reef

The Siskin Folk Club - a dedicated venue for sing-a-rounds, music sessions, and the festival choir will also host a Sunday morning multi-faith gathering

Workshops, including singing, songwriting, instruments and crafting

articles.title: Fermanagh barn owl success raises hopes for rare bird
articles.summary: Ten chicks have been successfully reared by two breeding pairs at secret sites across Fermanagh.
articles.body:
Barn owls have had a bumper summer in County Fermanagh, with 10 chicks recorded across two sites.

The breeding success follows years of conservation work by Ulster Wildlife with local farmers installing nest boxes and improving habitat for the elusive bird.

There are thought to be fewer than 30 breeding pairs left in Northern Ireland. The chicks have had rings placed on their legs so that they can be recorded in any other areas they turn up in after leaving the nest.

People are being encouraged to report any sightings of barn owls across Northern Ireland, particularly in the west, to help fill in gaps in the records and even help protect important breeding areas.

The Fermanagh chicks are thought to be the first recorded ones in the county for half a century.

Most of Ulster Wildlife's barn owl records come from the east of Northern Ireland.

The two broods of five chicks appeared in nest boxes that had been installed at different sites, after more than a decade of work with landowners.

The locations are being kept secret to help protect the rare, locally endangered bird.

Katy Bell, a senior conservation officer from Ulster Wildlife, said nest boxes play a part, but the willingness of farmers to adapt to the needs of the "magical, mystical" barn owl has been important too.

"We've been working closely with landowners, advising on land management and also putting up boxes," she said.

"So it's the combination of both - really you need nice thick hedgerows, lots of kind of rough areas and long grass for them to hunt over and then somewhere for them to nest. And that's really exciting."

The charity has worked closely with BirdWatch Ireland and has seen the population start to spread up from County Cavan.

The chicks have had small identification rings placed round their legs so that they can be traced when they are spotted again.

It is the first time chicks are known to have been ringed in Fermanagh under licence from the Northern Ireland Environment Agency, with support from the British Trust for Ornithology.

Over the past 50 years, barn owl numbers have declined across the UK.

The birds are now red-listed - classified as being at risk of extinction - largely due to a loss of habitat but also the use of pesticide.

Bell has been closely involved in the project to support barn owls.

"They face so many challenges," Bell said.

"They get poisoned with rodenticides, the loss of trees for them to nest in, the loss of nice big hedgerows for them to hunt over, the loss of rough ground for them to hunt over. They do get hit on our roads.

"They're just really up against it, so anything that we can do to create little safe havens for them here Is just they really need."

Those safe havens come in the form of nest boxes, specially designed to resemble the tree cavities barn owls nest in that are disappearing from our countryside.

Conservationists can access the nests to check on any chicks and ensure their wellbeing.

And there is a platform on the front, where the young birds will exercise and practise flying before leaving the nest.

Bell has "a long, long list" of farmers applying to have boxes installed.

"Of course, they're the farmer's friend - if you have them on the farm, that's free rodent control.

"They're eating your rats and your mice and everything on your farm.

"They work in harmony with us, which is just wonderful."

They usually nest in cavities that form in large, old trees like oaks.

And they need to be near rough ground that offers habitat for the small rodents they hunt.

But the number of the right type of tree near the right type of area is falling.

Bell said suburban back gardens are just not suitable.

"We either need barns - we put some in barns - or big, mature trees and open ground.

"So usually we go out and visit farms in the autumn, see if they're suitable and then if they are, we'll put up boxes in the winter time."

But people can still play a part in supporting barn owls by reporting sightings.

And Bell said the birds are a sight that cannot be forgotten.

They're actually quite small birds, about the size of a wood pigeon, but they look much bigger - they have a wingspan much bigger in comparison to most other birds to their body size.

"So you see them hovering over the field and you'll get this just big flash of white.

"And it's just like nothing else you'll see."

articles.title: US embassies across the world to visa applicants: Your visa application is on hold as our consular officers need to be ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Immigrant visa applicants across the world have been told that their applications are on hold as the Trump administration has launched a global traini.
articles.body: Immigrant visa applicants across the world have been told that their applications are on hold as the Trump administration has launched a global training initiative for consular officers. According to a report by Financial Times, the scheduled interviews at US embassies and consulates are now being rescheduled and the applicants are also receiving notices that the new dates will be provided later. A State Department spokesperson said the pause is meant to ensure officers can âevaluate every visa applicant comprehensively and consistently.â The training emphasizes screening out individuals deemed likely to become a public charge, or dependent on U.S. public benefits. âA more prosperous America means ensuring that visa applicants are not likely to become a public charge,â the spokesperson told the Financial Times.Why US embassies are emailing immigrant visa applicantsUS embassies and consulates have begun emailing immigrant visa applicants to inform them that their scheduled interview appointments are being rescheduled, with no new date provided â only a promise of future notice once a new time is set. The disruption is affecting applicants globally, from Mumbai to Naples, many of whom had already made costly, time-sensitive arrangements to attend their original appointments.The State Department's explanationA State Department spokesperson told the Financial Times the pause is tied to a newly launched "global training initiative" intended to ensure consular officers are fully equipped to evaluate every visa applicant comprehensively and consistently. The stated goal centers on public-charge screening â filtering out applicants deemed likely to become dependent on US public benefits. The spokesperson framed the effort as part of ensuring prosperity for the country by keeping out those unlikely to be self-sufficient under US law.The department did not offer a timeline for when appointments would resume, saying only that visa service scheduling would be adjusted to accommodate the training.Part of a broader immigration crackdownThe pause is the latest in a series of moves by an administration that has made restricting entry to the US a defining priority. President Trump has centered his presidency on cracking down on undocumented immigration while also tightening legal pathways â imposing new limits on visas and green cards and effectively ending nearly all refugee resettlement.The pause comes just days after a federal judge struck down a related Trump administration policy that had barred immigrant visa applications from nationals of 75, mostly lower-income, countries the administration considered likely to require public assistance. US District Judge Jeannette Vargas ruled that the ban â announced by the State Department in January â exceeded the administration's authority by overriding the discretion Congress assigned to consular officers in visa decision-making. Vargas struck down the policy along with any visa refusals issued under it, and gave both sides until September 11 to propose next steps in the litigation.The sequence has left some immigration attorneys questioning whether the new "training" pause is, functionally, a way to continue restricting the same pool of applicants after the original policy was struck down in court â though the State Department has not characterised it that way.The dilemma of visa applicantsAs per the FT report, Brian Simmons, an attorney at immigration law firm Fragomen in Washington, said many affected applicants had already spent thousands of dollars and upended their lives to attend interviews that were then canceled at the last minute. The disruption is especially acute for a specific group: since last year, the administration has required immigrant visa applicants to process their cases in their country of citizenship â even when they already live and work legally in the US, and even when they are married to American citizens or have American children. For that population, a canceled appointment can mean an extended, unplanned stay abroad, separated from family, jobs, and homes back in the US.Legal context: A long history of court battlesThis isn't the first time Trump's immigration policies have run into judicial pushback. Early in his first term, federal courts rolled back his attempt to bar entry to nationals of seven majority-Muslim countries, before the Supreme Court eventually allowed a scaled-back version of that policy to proceed. The current litigation over the 75-country visa ban suggests a similar legal fight may be ahead for whatever policy ultimately replaces or follows this new global pause.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Akash to Pralay: Why private missile manufacturing could be a game changer for India's defence readiness
articles.summary: News News: In a landmark push toward expanding self-reliance in defence manufacturing, the Centre has approved the transfer of Defence Research and Development O.
articles.body: In a landmark push toward expanding self-reliance in defence manufacturing, the Centre has approved the transfer of Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO)-developed technologies for all conventional missile systems to the Indian private industry. This has marked one of the most significant shifts in India's missile production model. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh cleared the decision, allowing qualified domestic companies to move beyond mere component supply and undertake full-scale, in-house production of missile systems for the first time.The conventional portfolio being thrown open is extensive, which according to sources covers Akash family of surface-to-air missiles, Very Short Range Air Defence System (VSHORADS), missiles of the Astra air-to-air family, Rudram anti-radiation missile, anti-tank systems including Nag and SANT, Man-Portable ATGM (MP-ATGM), Naval Anti-Ship Missile-Short Range (NASM-SR), Long Range Land-Attack Cruise Missiles (LR-LACM) and Pralay quasi-ballistic missile. Strategic missiles such as the Agni series and the K-series will not be made by the private industry. Weapons such as the Brahmos and the Medium Range Surface to Air Missile (MRSAM), jointly developed by Russia and Israel respectively, as they are governed by separate arrangements.This marks a clear departure from the decades-old model where DRDO handed over its missile designs almost exclusively to state-run Bharat Dynamics Limited for series production. Going forward, private firms will compete for technology licences through a bidding process, opening the field to companies such as Tata, Adani, Bharat Forge, Mahindra and ICOMM, all of whom are already contracted for various tactical missile and rocket programmes. The defence ministry states that the shift will strengthen the domestic industrial base, cut import dependence, boost MSME participation, and raise indigenous value addition, cementing India's transition from being primarily an importer to becoming a serious player in the global missile export market.DRDO-private industry partnership on the riseThe Development-cum-Production Partner (DcPP) model has quietly become one of the most consequential frameworks in India's push for self-reliance in defence manufacturing. Conceived by DRDO, it works on a simple principle, capable manufacturing partners are identified from both public and private sectors through competitive selection, and the technology needed to actually produce these systems is then transferred to them.The scale of this ecosystem is striking. DRDO now draws on a network of over 2,200 industries capable of producing sub-systems, systems and equipment. By March this year, 134 companies had signed on as DcPPs or Production Agencies, more than 2,180 technology transfer agreements had been inked, and upwards of 2,780 Intellectual Property Rights had been opened up for tthe private industry to use, till June this year. This marks a structural shift for a sector once concentrated almost entirely within public sector giants, where cutting-edge research often took years to reach the battlefield. The DcPP model has quietly built the industrial backbone behind India's broader defence manufacturing expansion.Why involving private industry mattersRecent and ongoing conflicts, such as those underway in Ukraine and in west Asia have demonstrated the importance of maintaining a significant weapons stockpile and the manufacturing capability to make these weapons at scale. The ability of private industry to manufacture these weapons at scale. The government's decision to transfer DRDO's conventional missile technologies to the private industry carries a clear set of advantages for the country's defence manufacturing sector. It allows missile systems to move directly from the drawing board into industrial-scale production, cutting the years-long lag that has often kept indigenous designs stuck at the prototype stage. It also breaks the near-monopoly enjoyed by state-run Bharat Dynamics Limited, whose production lines are already stretched thin by both domestic orders and a growing export pipeline.By opening the field to multiple qualified private players, the decision widens India's overall manufacturing capacity, while also pulling MSMEs deeper into the supply chain rather than restricting participation to large conglomerates alone. This, in turn, is expected to push up domestic value addition and reduce dependence on imported components, a long-standing weak point in India's defence ecosystem.Crucially, the move also builds surge capacity, giving India the industrial depth to scale up output quickly should a prolonged conflict demand it, while strengthening the country's hand in a defence export market where interest in systems like the Astra is already growing. For DRDO itself, offloading production duties frees up bandwidth to focus squarely on developing the next generation of weapons systems.Private missile production in IndiaEven before this week's technology transfer announcement, Indian private industry had already built a substantial missile manufacturing footprint. Tata Advanced Systems has been central to the Akash Air Force Launcher programme and produces MRSAM Army launchers mounted on its own HMV 8x8 vehicles, alongside supplying Pinaka rocket launchers and command posts under a two-decade public-private partnership with DRDO.Bharat Forge, through its subsidiary Kalyani Strategic Systems, has secured large Pinaka rocket contracts, including export orders to Armenia, and has been positioned as a serious contender for future strategic projects. Solar Defence and Aerospace has gone furthest in developing its own systems outright, the Nagastra loitering munition, used during Operation Sindoor, the Bhargavastra anti-drone salvo system, and the proposed Maheshwarastra precision rocket family, besides serving as production agency for guided Pinaka rockets.Adani Defence and Aerospace has developed the SR-1 loitering munition and VTOL-5 attack drone in-house, while also acting as a DRDO production partner for guided munitions and anti-radiation missiles. ICOMM Tele contributes missile guidance systems and sub-components, while Mahindra Defence's missile-adjacent work remains largely confined to naval systems such as torpedo launchers and anti-submarine suites, rather than missiles themselves. Adani also lists weapon systems such as VSHORAD, MR-SAM, Rudram-1 and UAV Launched Precision Guided Missile (ULPGM) on its website.
