articles.title: A San Francisco woman hires a humanoid robot for $30 an hour to clean her apartment while controlling it remotely from her sofa
articles.summary: US News: A San Francisco woman has given a glimpse of what home cleaning could look like in the age of humanoid robots after hiring one for $30 an hour to work.
articles.body: A San Francisco woman has given a glimpse of what home cleaning could look like in the age of humanoid robots after hiring one for $30 an hour to work inside her apartment. Gianna Capezio booked a one-hour cleaning visit from San Francisco startup Tau Robotics, with the humanoid robot vacuuming, making her bed and cleaning her bathroom during the session. The robot was not operating autonomously. A trained human operator controlled it remotely through its cameras, with artificial intelligence assisting the system. Capezio said the robot was slower than a human cleaner but still did a solid job and she did not have to redo its work afterwards. Her video of the unusual cleaning session quickly spread online, attracting millions of views and sparking debate over the technology, its usefulness and the future of household work.San Francisco woman hires a humanoid robot for a $30 cleaning visitCapezio's experience came after Tau Robotics began offering its humanoid cleaning service to selected customers in San Francisco. The company currently operates the service on an invite-only basis, with customers paying a flat $30 for a one-hour visit. Tau advertises its robots for tasks including vacuuming, wiping surfaces, taking out rubbish and clearing light clutter, while its current service also offers options for kitchen, bathroom and deeper cleaning. Customers cannot simply leave the robot alone inside an empty property. Tau's terms require the customer or another authorised adult to remain at home throughout the visit, and the company does not accept keys, lockboxes or door codes. The robot also depends on a working internet connection and electricity because it is operated remotely. The service is therefore still an early-stage experiment rather than a conventional autonomous cleaning business, but it represents a notable step because a humanoid machine is now being sent into real homes to perform paid household work.A human operator controls the robot remotelyThe most important part of Tau's system is that the humanoid is not yet capable of independently cleaning an entire home. Tau's own terms state that the robot is operated in real time by a trained human operator working from the company's facility, while AI assists with the robot's operation. Tau says its robots are jointly operated by humans and AI, with the balance between direct human control and higher-level guidance varying depending on the task. The company's long-term objective is to reduce that dependence and eventually have its robots perform more of the work autonomously. That makes the current service different from a fully independent household robot. A person is effectively guiding the machine while the customer watches it carry out physical tasks inside the home. The approach also allows Tau to gather information from real cleaning sessions that can be used to improve its AI models. In that sense, today's $30 cleaning visit is both a household service and a real-world test of how humanoid robots behave in unpredictable domestic environments.The robot can vacuum, wipe surfaces and handle everyday choresTau's humanoids are designed to perform relatively straightforward household tasks rather than every job a human cleaner might undertake. The company says its robots can vacuum floors, wipe surfaces, take out rubbish and move ordinary objects such as chairs and laundry baskets to clean around them. Tau also advertises specialised cleaning options, including kitchen and bathroom work and deeper cleaning involving areas such as baseboards, grout and window tracks. There are clear restrictions, however. The robot does not climb ladders, work outside the home, handle biohazards or pest infestations, move heavy furniture or appliances, or handle firearms, medication, drug paraphernalia or cash. Bedrooms and bathrooms are excluded from a standard booking unless the customer specifically opts them in. Capezio's experience showed that the technology can already complete several recognisable household chores, although she noted that the robot moved more slowly than a human cleaner. That limitation is also visible in footage of Tau's robots, whose deliberate movements highlight how far current humanoid robotics still has to go before machines can match the speed and adaptability of experienced human cleaners.Cameras inside homes raise a major privacy questionThe service also introduces an unusual privacy issue because the remote operator needs to see what the robot sees. Tau's privacy policy states that the robot continuously records video through cameras mounted on its head and wrists during a cleaning visit, while the human operator watches the live feed. Tau says the robot's microphones are disabled, meaning it does not record or listen to audio inside the home, although the operator can speak through the robot's speaker. The company says recorded video, robot telemetry and operator commands are also used to train its AI models. Its terms state that footage is retained and may be reviewed by Tau staff, engineers and contracted service providers involved in storage, processing, data labelling and model development. Customers must therefore agree to continuous recording as part of using the service, and anyone else living in the home should be informed before the robot arrives. The company says customers can designate areas as off-limits and anyone present can ask the operator to stop the session at any time. These rules make privacy one of the most important considerations surrounding the service, particularly because the technology is designed to operate inside some of the most private spaces people have.The $30 robot cleaner is really a test of the future of home roboticsCapezio's cleaning session has attracted attention because it turns a futuristic idea into something people can actually try. Her video reportedly received millions of views, with reactions ranging from amusement about the robot's slow movements to scepticism about whether it can genuinely compete with a human cleaner. UC Berkeley robotics professor Ken Goldberg has also questioned whether current humanoids are ready to perform useful household cleaning at scale, pointing to the difficulty of manipulating everyday objects and cleaning awkward surfaces. Tau's founders acknowledge that current AI cannot fully control a humanoid in the way the company ultimately wants. Yet the experiment is significant because the robots are now being exposed to real homes rather than carefully controlled demonstrations. At $30 an hour, the service is designed to make that experiment accessible to customers while giving Tau opportunities to collect real-world data and improve its systems. The current robot may still need a human operator, move slowly and work within strict limits, but the larger goal is clear. articles.body: Amazon has announced that it will shut down its crowdsourced work platform Mechanical Truk, effective September 30, 2026, as reported by CNBC. Launched in the year 2025, the service was described by founder Jeff Bezos has âartificial artificial intelligenceâ, outsourcing simple digital tasks to humans that computers struggled to complete. The platform managed to connect hundreds of thousands of workers, known as âtrukersâ, to small jobs such as labelling data, transcribing audio, or answering surveys. At its peak, the platform served more than 500,000 workers. But with the rise of advanced AI models and competing data-labeling startups like Scale AI, Mercor, and Prolific, MTurk had been in decline.Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' âartificial artificial intelligenceâAmazon founder Jeff Bezos famously described the service as "artificial artificial intelligence," a nod to how it used human labor to complete tasks that machines of the era simply couldn't manage on their own. The platform's name is a reference to the original Mechanical Turk, an 18th-century chess-playing automaton that appeared to operate autonomously but was secretly controlled by a hidden human chess master. Amazon reportedly first conceived of the platform to help label the vast troves of data generated by its own online store.From half a million workers to a platform 'in decline'At its peak, Mechanical Turk served more than 500,000 workers, often referred to as "turkers." But the platform's fortunes have shifted dramatically in recent years. Krista Pawloski, a data worker and organizer with Turkopticon â an advocacy group for data workers â said MTurk had been in decline as the broader AI training landscape moved on without it. Since the platform's 2005 launch, AI models have advanced enormously, and a new wave of specialized data-labeling startups, including Scale AI, Mercor, and Prolific, have emerged to recruit workers for AI model training, pulling volume away from Amazon's original platform.Amazon's later pivot toward AI training dataAs demand for AI training data grew, Amazon tried to reposition Mechanical Turk as a data-annotation source for its SageMaker machine learning service, marketing the platform's round-the-clock worker availability as a way to get fast turnaround on human review and labeling tasks. But Pawloski said Amazon appeared to invest fewer resources into improving the platform even as competition intensified, prompting many turkers to migrate to rival services instead.Questions about data qualityThe platform's reliability has also faced scrutiny. A 2023 academic study out of Switzerland found that up to 46% of Mechanical Turk workers were using AI models themselves to complete supposedly human-generated tasks â a finding that complicates the value of MTurk-sourced data for training AI systems that are, in some cases, being used to generate that very data.A two-decade career built on turkingFor some workers, Mechanical Turk wasn't a side gig â it was a livelihood. Pawloski began turking in 2008 while on maternity leave, using it as supplemental income, before shifting to the work full-time in 2012 after losing her job and needing flexibility to care for her son, who has special needs. She began organizing with Turkopticon in 2019; the group originally focused specifically on Mechanical Turk workers before broadening its scope to data workers more generally.Pawloski said platforms like Mechanical Turk have long provided meaningful income and flexible, remote work comparable to other gig economy jobs like ride-hailing or Amazon Flex delivery â with the added advantage of being completable from a smartphone. She said a small but dedicated group of workers still rely on the platform as a full-time job, and are now facing real uncertainty about what comes next.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: 'Hijab on their heads, not minds': Owaisi calls Allahabad HC ruling 'attack on Islam'
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi on Tuesday criticised the Allahabad High Court's dismissal of a minor student's petition seeking permissio.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi on Tuesday criticised the Allahabad High Court's dismissal of a minor student's petition seeking permission to wear a hijab with her prescribed school uniform in Prayagraj. Calling the ruling an "attack on Islam", Owaisi questioned the court's authority to determine what is essential to the religion.Addressing the Jalsa-e-Rahmatul-lil-Alameen gathering at the AIMIM headquarters in Darussalam, Hyderabad, Owaisi said the ruling was inconsistent with the constitutional protections of religious freedom and freedom of expression. He also pointed to the ongoing Sabarimala case before the Supreme Court, where a nine-judge bench is examining questions surrounding essential religious practices.The AIMIM chief said, "A judgment came from the Allahabad high court. A girl was wearing a hijab to school, and the Court ruled that one cannot wear a hijab. I disagree with this High Court judgment; I do not concur with it. The Sabarimala case is already before the Supreme Court, where nine judges are deciding what is essential. Today's verdict violates Articles 25 and 19 of the Indian Constitution. Who are you to decide what is essential to Islam? Girls are wearing hijab on their heads, not on their minds. It is an attack on Islam."The remarks came after a division bench of Justices JJ Munir and Indrajit Shukla dismissed the student's petition challenging the school's refusal to allow her to wear a scarf over her uniform.The court observed that the petitioner had not produced religious scriptures or other material establishing that wearing a scarf was an "essential" part of her religion, such that its absence would affect her faith. It also noted that photographs submitted before the court showed other students from the same religious community attending the school without scarves.The bench held that where a dress code is uniform, non-discriminatory, adopted in good faith and intended to maintain discipline and institutional identity, determining the uniform primarily falls within the school's jurisdiction.The court further said that the student's previous practice of wearing a scarf in lower classes without objection did not create a permanent or enforceable right to require the school to alter its uniform policy. It clarified that the school was not curtailing her freedom of faith but was enforcing institutional discipline, with the uniform forming an essential part of that discipline.The student had completed Class 10 at the same school and sought admission to Class 11. She told the court that she had worn a scarf over her school uniform since Class 6 and that the school had never objected to it.However, when she sought admission to Class 11, the school management informed her that wearing a scarf violated its dress code and refused admission on that ground.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Libyan cleared after Lockerbie bombing trial dies aged 70
articles.summary: A Facebook post by Libyan Airlines announced the death of Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah and expressed the company's condolences to his family.
articles.body:
A Libyan who was cleared after standing trial over the Lockerbie bombing is reported to have died aged 70.

Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah was accused of murdering 270 people in the attack on Pan Am Flight 103 in December 1988.

He was found not guilty but a second Libyan, Abdulbasset Al Megrahi, was convicted of playing a key role in the bombing of the American airliner.

A Facebook post by Libyan Airlines announced his death and expressed the company's condolences to his family.

Fhimah worked for the carrier in Malta before the bombing of Pan Am 103.

The charges against Fhimah and Megrahi were first announced by Scotland and the United States in 1991.

Years of sanctions imposed on Libya by the United Nations led to the two men being handed over to stand trial at a Scottish court sitting in the Netherlands.

In 2001, three judges convicted Megrahi of mass murder and jailed him for life, but found Fhimah not guilty.

Megrahi died from cancer in 2012, after being freed on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government.

Fhimah always denied any involvement and was welcomed home to Libya by the country's late dictator Colonel Muammar Gaddafi.

In 2022, the FBI revealed that he had been implicated in the case again, through an alleged confession made by another Libyan who is facing trial in the United States.

Abu Agila Mohammad Masud Kheir Al-Marimi is said to have told a Libyan police officer that he took part in a plot to bomb the plane along with Fhimah and Megrahi, when all three were members of the Libyan intelligence service.

Al-Marimi has denied making the bomb that brought down the jumbo jet and claims the confession is false and was made under duress.

The contents of Al-Marimi's alleged confession and other new evidence which has emerged from Libya has led to speculation that Fhimah could have faced a second trial over the attack on the airliner.

The indictment against Fhimah announced by the US Government in 1991 is still outstanding.

Under the Double Jeopardy (Scotland) Act 2011 , external , a suspect can be tried over the same crime a second time, if there is new evidence - which was not available during the original trial - that substantially strengthens the case against them.

The BBC understands Scottish and US prosecutors would have looked at taking fresh action against Fhimah, if Al-Marimi was convicted by the court in Washington.

But pursuing a prosecution in Scotland or the US would have been legally challenging and politically sensitive, given his acquittal by the Scottish court in 2001.

Al Marimi is now due to stand trial in Washington in January, after a federal court judge agreed to postpone the case for a third time.

The delay, requested by the defence, followed the emergence of "newly discovered" evidence on the case.

The postponement was not connected to Fhimah's reported death.

articles.title: How Stephen Curry played a huge role in Golden State Warriors’ first new signing of the offseason
articles.summary: The Golden State Warriors spent over two months of the 2026 offseason without signing a single new player to their roster before finally making an addition o...
articles.body:
The Golden State Warriors spent over two months of the 2026 offseason without signing a single new player to their roster before finally making an addition on August 25.

The Warriors spent most of their offseason recruiting LeBron James , a pursuit that failed. The team has been quiet since then, but made two late-August signings to bolster their roster before the season.

Guard Brandon Williams and forward Georges Niang both signed on minimum contracts with the franchise, with Stephen Curry specifically playing a crucial role in one of them joining the Warriors.

Stephen Curry recruited new signing Brandon Williams on a Zoom call

The SF Chronicle spoke to Toby Spino, Williams' coach and advisor, and revealed that Curry pitched Brandon on joining the Warriors a few months ago.

"Golden State has had a target on Williams for months. Earlier this summer… Stephen Curry set up a call with Williams to talk shop. 'When he first came in, he was like, 'Oh, I gotta go home. I got a Zoom call with Wardell.'"

Despite the call being months ago, Williams was left in a state of limbo as the Warriors were in the middle of their LeBron pursuit at the time.

Now, after a summer of primarily bringing back the roster that missed the playoffs last season, Williams became the Warriors' first addition of the summer, beating Georges Niang to that honor by a few hours.

Williams will be a backup rotational guard for the Warriors behind Curry and De'Anthony Melton. While his role depends on how the season plays out, this is a high-upside signing by GSW.

Brandon Williams' 2025-26 stats before joining the Warriors

Williams averaged 13.0 points and 3.9 assists on 47.2% from the field and 23.2% from three for the Mavericks last season.

He is a true NBA developmental story, going undrafted but staying on a two-way contract with the Mavericks for multiple seasons before finally getting a breakout opportunity last season.

His poor three-point shooting held the Mavericks back from extending him and warded off other teams looking for low-usage rotational players to stretch the floor.

The Warriors have enough floor-spacing and need genuine driving threats from the perimeter who can collapse defenses while also having the scoring touch to create their own opportunities.

Williams is also an above-average defender despite being 6'2″, primarily due to his hustle and intensity. He's a great rotational fit for the Warriors and could have a breakout season if his shot has improved, given that the Warriors have opportunities for guards like him to come in and succeed.

Hello everyone, and welcome to the live blog for the Sri Lanka vs India 1st Test in Galle.

Sri Lanka vs India, 2nd Test, Day 4: Live updates and scorecard

Eight wickets needed for India to seal it, while Sri Lanka have to find another 130 runs just to clear the deficit and make the visitors chase. The deck isn't playing any crazy tricks, yet there's enough nip and turn to stop anyone from ever feeling truly set.

For the hosts, it's all about testing Indian stamina. The visitors have already toiled through 111.4 overs across the past two days. Drag this out with a couple of gritty, long-drawn stands, and fatigue could well become a factor.

Pasindu Sooriyabandara has looked in fine touch on 35, while Kamindu Mendis is eager to snap a quiet run and make a statement before the series wraps up. A serious test of character ahead for this batting lineup.

Back in a flash for the post-lunch session!

SL fail to save follow-on! Dinusha is trapped at slips by Rahul off Suthar. India have enforced the follow-on, which means Sri Lanka must come out to bat once again.

Sonal Dinusha scores his second Test century, and Jaiswal is the first Indian to clap while standing in gully. SL still need 21 runs to avoid follow-on.

Sri Lanka vs India, 2nd Test, Day 3: Live updates and scorecard

Stumps: Sri Lanka still have a long way to go

The hosts still need 38 runs needed to avoid the follow-on as Suthar and Krishna ripped through the Sri Lankan batting lineup with three wickets apiece.

Dinusha remains the only man standing between a total collapse with the all-rounder nearing his second century in as many matches.

The hosts have somewhat reduced the margin but they are still 87 runs short of avoiding follow-on.

Pasindu Sooriyabandara misses out on his century as Sri Lanka's collapse continues.

After the setback at the end of Day 2, the hosts show great fight in the first session as they cross the 100-run mark.

The hosts were in trouble at the end of Day 2 of the series decider in Colombo. Sri Lankan batters will hope to bat all through Day 3 to stand a chance of saving the game.

Sri Lanka vs India, 2nd Test, Day 2: Live updates and scorecard

A touch of late drama rounded off a rain-shortened second day. Dhruv Jurel's century carried India past the 500 mark, prompting the declaration. Weather had already eaten up two hours of the morning session, and further showers interrupted Sri Lanka's innings later on.

Once play resumed, Prasidh Krishna and Manav Suthar made quick inroads with a wicket each, leaving the hosts in early trouble at 8/2 before the umpires called time.

Jurel gets his century, and then rain stops play

Jurel took 22 balls to get to his 100 from 99. However, it was worth the wait. It was a gem of an innings, and India declared at 503/9. Sri Lanka come out to bat but bad light stops play.

Rain forces play stoppage as Jurel nears milestone

Stoppage due to rain forced an early tea as Dhruv Jurel nears his sophomore century. Batting at 95, the all-rounder has completely grounded India's innings after a flurry of wickets nearly threatened to end the visitor's play in the second innings.

However, with sheets covering the pitch and rain coming down heavily, he might need to wait a bit more for his milestone.

Pant was finally dismissed, once again missing out on a century while Prabath Jayasuriya quickly sent Manav Suthar back to the dressing room to get Sri Lanka's eighth wicket.

Jurel continues to hold India's innings from one end as the hosts hope to wrap up the visitors within this session.

A blundering partnership between the two tailenders

India is looking to build up towards a big score as the visitors go for lunch at 419/6. Both Pant and Jurel continue to find boundaries as the initial scare of Fernando has made way for quick runs. The Indian wicketkeeper seems particularly eager for a big score after his playing time was cut short on Day 1.

Pant returned to the crease after Jain's dismissal and quickly put the pedal to the metal. The duo bagged their second half-centuries of the series while also helping India breach the 400-run mark.

Fernando gets an early breakthrough for Sri Lanka

The fast bowler bowls it short, forcing Jain to go for a flick landing straight on his left at the gully as Kamil Mishara completes the catch. This is Fernando's fourth wicket as the hosts look to quickly dismiss India.

Sri Lanka vs India, 2nd Test, Day 1: Live updates and scorecard

India ends day 1 with 300 runs on the board

India ends the day with 300 runs on the board with Dhruv Jurel and Saransh Hain on the crease for the guests. Sri Lanka was able to dismiss Jadeja just before stumps, giving Fernando his third wicket of the day.

Keshara Nuwantha has ended Devdutt Padikkal's stay on 117 off 193 balls, a huge wicket for Sri Lanka with the second new ball just around the corner. Pushed through quicker on a flatter trajectory, it was a delivery Padikkal should have come forward to. Instead, he went right back, and the ball gripped, turned past the outside edge and crashed into the off stump.

The RCB star conjured his second Test century in the space of a week, reaching three figures off 168 balls with a single eased down to long-on off Prabath Jayasuriya. He had moved into the nineties in style, backing away to hammer a short, wide delivery through cover before flashing another gorgeous cut through the same region to reach 99.

Pant's misfortune with injuries continues as he has been forced to retire hurt. In the first ball of the 58th over, Lahiru Kamara's delivery hit Pant on his left forearm, which forced him to leave the pitch in immense pain.

Having survived a massive scare on the very first delivery, Devdutt Padikkal has looked dialled in ever since. He raised his half-century with a crisp, well-placed drive wide of cover. The batters initially took off thinking two, only to see the ball speed all the way to the boundary cushion. Up at the other end, Shubman Gill strolled to a fifty of his own. But soon after that, he was dismissed after edging one to Dickwella.

Padikkal and Gill stich a quality partnership

Things are ticking along smoothly for India. Shubman Gill and Devdutt Padikkal haven't taken any silly chances, but they've still kept the scoreboard moving at a nice, healthy rate. Their 50-run stand took 96 deliveries to assemble: measured, calm, and sensible.

There's definitely still some purchase out there if the pacers bend their backs, but Sri Lanka's fast bowlers have barely had a bowl this session. Hard to blame them entirely, given the brutal Colombo heat sapping everyone's energy out in the middle.

Two early dismissals, spilt chances in the field, and a helmet butt from Jaiswal made for a chaotic, action-packed opening session. Even so, India has kept the scoreboard ticking at a healthy clip above 3.5 an over. However, Shubman Gill and Devdutt Padikkal will know they need to tread carefully once play resumes after the break.

It has been a careful start from the hosts. The Sri Lankan pacers are asking some serious questions, and KL Rahul and Jaiswal have been in trouble on a couple of occasions, with the odd ball jagging back in.

Spin has still had the upper hand recently, as spinners have picked up 45 wickets across the last three Tests here, compared to 35 for the pacers.

India arrive full of confidence following their commanding 165-run win in the series opener. Devdutt Padikkal, KL Rahul, and Manav Suthar were the standout contributors in Galle. Sri Lanka couldn't dodge the follow-on after all. Dinusha edged one off Manav Suthar, and KL Rahul made no mistake, pouching a clean catch in the slips to wrap things up.

Sri Lanka are still 87 runs short of avoiding a follow-on as India continue to enjoy the upper hand.

Pasindu departs for 80 runs after a brilliant knock as Sri Lanka are now staring at follow-on.

After the setback at the end of Day 2, the hosts show great fight in the first session as the cross the 100-run mark.

Sri Lanka would hope to quickly dismiss the visitors come day 2.

Padikkal's marathon stay finally ended on 117 from 193 balls, bowled by Keshara Nuwantha in the over before the second new ball became available. Jadeja and Padikkal have picked up where Pant left off, ticking the score along without any alarms. The left-hander reached his second Test century in the space of a week, getting there off 168 balls with a single eased down to long-on, and celebrated by removing his helmet to acknowledge the dressing room.

He had moved into the nineties in style, backing away to hammer Jayasuriya through cover before flashing another cut through the same region. Sri Lanka's bowlers, already warned once for a slow over rate, are running out of ideas in the Colombo heat.

Rishabh Pant has been forced to leave the pitch after being hit on his left forearm. The Indian wicketkeeper was visibly in pain as he walked off the pitch. Pant's misfortune with injuries continues.

Padikkal got a huge reprieve off the very first ball, but since then he has looked like a man on a mission. He has brought up his 50 with a well-timed drive wide of cover. It started as a call for a double before he looked up and saw it had raced away to the rope.

At the other end, Shubman Gill has notched up his half-century as well. But a reckless shot at a ball outside off stump and he has to walk back.

So far so good for India. Gill and Padikkal have been playing risk-free cricket and yet managing to get the runs. The half-century partnership arrived off 96 balls. The pitch still has a bit of spice for the quicks, but they've hardly bowled. The sweltering heat in Colombo probably isn't helping.

A couple of wickets down, a couple of catches down, and a helmet-butt from Jaiswal, and it was an eventful morning session. India are still scoring above 3.5 rpo, but Gill & Padikkal would be cautious when they come out in the second session.

A watchful beginning by the home side. The Sri Lankan fast bowlers are posing tough questions up front, and both KL Rahul and Yashasvi Jaiswal have had uncomfortable moments with the ball darting sharply back off the seam.

articles.title: Joshua Zirkzee Key To Man Utd Transfers As Interest Remains
articles.summary: Joshua Zirkzee’s potential return to Italy holds the key to Manchester United’s recruitment plans as Michael Carrick targets a new striker to solve his side'...
articles.body:
Why Man United have always needed a striker this summer.

On the field, Manchester United could not have had a worse start to the season, with a 2-0 loss to newly-promoted Hull City.

In almost every regard, the Tigers outperformed the Red Devils, which will leave Michael Carrick with many tactical headaches.

Off the field, United could be braced for a very busy week with the transfer deadline on the 1st of September on the horizon.

In terms of incomings, Carlos Baleba has now completed his move from Brighton and Hove Albion . His first words as a Manchester United player can be found here .

Outgoings could be key for United if they want to bring in more players, as the futures of some senior squad and academy players are pivotal to the club.

Joshua Zirkzee has been linked with a move away all summer, with the same Serie A clubs hovering around the player but yet to make a formal offer. However, with the transfer deadline approaching, a deal may be more likely to advance.

According to Laurie Whitwell, the likes of Juventus and Como have shown clear interest in bringing the Dutchman back to Italy , where he excelled at Bologna .

He also reported that three other unnamed Premier League clubs are interested in him. One of those clubs could be Aston Villa , with the Midlands club looking for a striker and having previously been linked with the centre forward.

The departure of Zirkzee is so important because Whitwell also suggested that if the Dutchman did leave, the club could return to the market for a striker to deputise for or compete with Benjamin Sesko .

Lisandro Martinez's Suddenly 'Fighting' To Save Career Amid Man Utd Hierarchy DoubtsPersistent injury woes may force Manchester United to offload Lisandro Martinez, as club officials demand the Argentine proves his fitness before the summer transfer window shuts.

Zirkzee is undoubtedly a good footballer with a lot of talent, but the Dutchman has failed to adapt to life at Old Trafford, meaning a departure is best for all parties.

Against Hull City and at times last season, it was abundantly clear that without a real focal point up front, the team looked lost. While Matheus Cunha (who started up front against Hull), Bryan Mbeumo , and Marcus Rashford can play there, they lack the instincts and presence of an out-and-out striker.

When Sesko came on against Hull, it was clear that the impact of having a player consistently making those runs, even if the players could not find him, was hugely beneficial.

Whether it is an experienced player like Jean-Philippe Mateta or a riskier option like the youthful Nicolò Tresoldi , a striker is needed.

articles.title: Sugar prices: Why India is importing the sweetener for the first time in nearly a decade
articles.summary: Domestic sugar prices have jumped nearly 40%, forcing India to import 1 million tonnes of the sweetener.
articles.body:
India, the world's largest consumer of sugar, is trying to avoid a bittersweet festive season.

Sugar prices have jumped nearly 40% in the past two months, prompting the government to import 1 million tonnes for the first time in nearly a decade.

The move comes as demand surges from August, with festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi, Dussehra and Diwali leading into the busy wedding season. Food and beverage companies also begin stocking up for one of their busiest sales periods, adding pressure on wholesale prices.

Production is now expected to be 30.6 million tonnes in the current season, which runs from October 2025 to September 2026 - 11% below the government's earlier estimate of 34.3 million tonnes.

The squeeze has sent prices soaring. A kilo of sugar that cost around 40-45 rupees ($0.42-0.47; £0.31-0.35) in May-June was selling for more than 58-60 rupees in several markets in August, although prices have begun to ease slightly.

But how did a country, which is also the world's second-largest sugar producer, end up needing imports?

The government has blamed lower sugarcane production linked to reduced rainfall during El Niño, hoarding and tighter global supplies after adverse weather hit other major producers.

But experts say another key factor was that India overestimated its own production - and allowed sugar to be exported before the extent of the shortfall became clear.

The government initially approved exports of 1.5 million tonnes this season, adding another 500,000 tonnes in February. Nearly 800,000 tonnes had been shipped before exports were halted in May.

"From allowing exports at the start of the season to ending with an import of a million tonnes is a large variation on production estimates - and that's a big surprise," said Vikram Suryavanshi, a senior analyst at PhillipCapital India.

That matters because India has little sugar to spare. It consumed more than 28 million tonnes last season, not far below what it expects to produce this year.

Nearly three million tonnes is also expected to be diverted to ethanol production, leaving little room for any shortfall.

That is where the imports will help provide a buffer, says Atul Chaturvedi, non-executive director of Shree Renuka Sugars, India's largest sugar refiner and a major ethanol producer.

For three months from 1 September, sugar refineries in special economic zones near ports - which normally import raw sugar, refine it and re-export it - will be allowed to sell duty-free sugar in the domestic market.

The last time India imported sugar for domestic consumption was nearly a decade ago, when the country was grappling with drought.

Other measures are also under way. The Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA) has asked mills to begin crushing cane a fortnight earlier than usual to build stocks as the new harvest starts arriving in October.

But that crop, too, faces risks from erratic weather.

Sugarcane is highly water-intensive, and uneven monsoon rains and prolonged dry spells in key growing states such as Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka have affected the crop. Yields are expected to fall, while thinner cane with lower sucrose content means less sugar can be produced.

"Looking at the climate conditions, the next season is also not going to be a bumper crop, although it is too early for actual assessment," Chaturvedi said.

India has frequently restricted agricultural exports when domestic supplies tighten and prices rise. In 2023, for instance, it banned exports of non-basmati white rice for more than a year after crop damage contributed to rising food prices.

But experts say the failure to anticipate the sugar shortfall before allowing exports has raised questions about the government's forecasts.

"This year, the initial projections for sugarcane production did not materialise due to unusual weather in some parts and disease in certain varieties," said Siraj Hussain, a former secretary at the federal agriculture ministry.

The government has not explained why the scale of the shortfall was not identified before exports were halted on 13 May. It has said production fell below estimates because of sugarcane disease and waterlogging caused by excessive rainfall.

The BBC has contacted the agriculture ministry for comment.

Some commentators have also blamed the diversion of sugarcane to ethanol production for the shortage in a deficit year. Even earlier, sugar mills would set aside around 10% of their output for this, helping stabilise prices in times of excess production.

But India making E20, or petrol blended with 20% ethanol, the standard fuel at pumps this year, just as sugar output is low, has added to the challenge, experts say.

The government disputes how much the policy is to blame. It says the share of cane diverted to ethanol has fallen from 12% in 2022-23 to around 9% in 2025-26, and argues that weak production, hoarding and tighter global supplies are behind the sugar price surge.

Some in the industry agree. Deepak Ballani of the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA), which represents private mills producing nearly half of India's sugar, says stocks and monthly quotas for sugar released into the market are comfortable. He argues speculation and hoarding, rather than a genuine shortage, are driving prices higher.

The government has capped stocks held by traders and wholesalers at 400 tonnes for three months to curb hoarding.

Suryavanshi, however, disagrees. India has used such measures before, he says, yet prices continued to climb after the latest restrictions were announced. To him, that points to a real supply squeeze.

And India's decision to import comes as supplies are tightening globally.

El Niño has affected rainfall in Thailand, while heavy rain has disrupted cane harvesting in Brazil, the world's largest sugar producer, where mills are also diverting more cane to ethanol. Heatwaves have battered Europe's sugar beet crop, with France expecting its worst harvest in four years.

US government forecasters expect global production to fall to 184.9 million tonnes this season, from a record 186.1 million tonnes the year before.

London white sugar futures hit $541 a tonne in mid-August, their highest since April 2025, while New York raw sugar futures jumped 4% on the day India announced its imports.

For India, however, sugar availability could improve next year if high prices prompt mills to divert less cane to ethanol.

"At current sugar prices, it simply doesn't make economic sense for mills to divert cane juice to ethanol, so India's sugar scenario should be quite all right going forward," Chaturvedi said.

But the bigger lesson from this year's squeeze, he added, is clear: it is a "warning that going forward, we need to be a lot more careful in estimating our sugar crop numbers".

articles.body:
Roma was ready to welcome Jayden Oosterwolde to Trigoria yesterday.

The Dutchman arrived in Rome this morning, landing at Ciampino Airport on a flight from Amsterdam to begin his Giallorossi adventure.

articles.title: What happens when an athlete has a life-changing accident?
articles.summary: Saffron Cresswell was a promising eventer before a fall left her paralysed. Just eight months after first sitting in a canoe, she is heading to the Worlds.
articles.body:
After four months in hospital, Saffron Cresswell was dreading coming home.

Before she had the fall that would leave her paralysed at the age of 23, she had 25 horses that she trained and rode in a business she had been running since she was 15 and was a talented eventer on a pathway towards the Olympics.

Eight years earlier her parents had sold their house to buy a yard to support her career, with the family living in two tiny touring caravans for six years before they converted part of a barn into a home.

For years, Cresswell had been up at 5am, riding four ponies before school, then more afterwards - if she even went in. She puts her school attendance at "68% or something ridiculous" because she was "so busy riding".

'Busy' in fact turns out to be a common theme with Cresswell. During rehab at the hospital, she'd be waiting outside the gym for it to open so she could get an hour in before her physio session was even due to start.

There had only been five days during the four months where she hadn't had a visitor and so when she finally returned home to Worcestershire, where the horses had all been sold, reality was anything but hectic.

"I came home and fundamentally the next day, both my parents went out the door and went to work," says the now 25-year-old Cresswell. "So, I was home alone in a house that I couldn't really get out of and I couldn't really do anything."

There was only one thing for it: find a new sport. Little did she know that within eight months of sitting in a canoe for the first time, she would be heading for a World Championships.

Cresswell started riding when she was three, introduced to the sport by her mum, who was "horsey" but "doing low-level amateur stuff".

"I was the only child at primary school that was allowed a phone because I used to cycle from my primary school to the yard so I could start riding before my mum came home from work," she says.

She got into eventing "properly" at 13 when she produced her own young pony from beginners level to eventually representing Great Britain at three European championships.

She glances at the medals on her wall, saying: "One gold and two team silvers... so that sort of sparked the whole eventing career."

Then came the leap of faith from her parents - "much to my poor brother's trauma who was not horsey in any way" and was suddenly now sharing a caravan with his older sister - and Cresswell began running the business of riding and competing horses for other people and coaching.

Since her accident, she has not been back on a horse. Nor does she intend to.

"Because I'd done it so seriously and to such a high level that every day was about perfecting my technique and being better, I think, to get back on and not be able to do that physically, but also not even feel the horse underneath me, I think it would just be very disheartening for me," she says.

Instead, she coaches, which she says has helped her with what has turned out - surprisingly to her - the thing she would miss the most about pre-accident life.

"[What I miss] is literally just having the horse on the yard, to just go and like say 'hello' to them over the stable," she says. "And that comes from somebody who was so busy that I didn't really have loads of time to do that anyway."

The coaching is one of the new parts of the family business, which has had to change since her accident.

"The business is basically having to diversify, which is still very much an ongoing process," she says.

"My parents had given up so much to build something that allowed me to do the sport. It wasn't like we were at home and I left home and did this - they were very invested as well. So it's kind of affected everybody from that side of things."

Cresswell had been beginning to make her mark at senior level when she was competing at Bramham Horse Trials on 8 June, 2024.

Three fences before the end of her under-25 cross-country round, she came off her horse Vivendi Hero.

"I remember all of it because I didn't even get knocked out," she says. "[It was] just a freak accident.

"I just landed on the back of my head and unfortunately broke my back at T4 level - so chest level - and basically as soon as I fell, instantly knew I couldn't feel my legs."

She remembers an "awful" 45-minute ambulance ride to Leeds General Infirmary, where she had emergency surgery.

At that point, she wondered whether the damage would be permanent, because only couple of weeks previously she had been chatting to a friend - Olympic silver medallist Nicola Wilson - who had broken her neck in a fall.

"She said, 'when I fell, I couldn't feel my arm for 20 minutes, and then my feeling came back'. So when I had my accident, I had this really weird thing, like I just thought, 'oh, it's fine, it'll be 20 minutes, and my feeling will come back'," she says.

Wilson, who visited Cresswell in intensive care, regained her feeling in her legs in three or four weeks.

"So I have this really weird thing because then I was sort of waiting for three to four weeks as if I was going to get feeling back," says Cresswell, who was moved to a spinal unit in Wakefield.

"It was probably not until about six weeks that the realisation really hits... that actually this wasn't going to be the outcome that I had hoped for."

Cresswell was bedbound for six weeks in what she calls her "hotel room", a private room in the hospital where the wall was covered in get-well-soon cards.

Even then, she kept busy as the physios would give her some weights she could use for her arms.

"They were tiny, but in my head, it was a principle of having something to do every day," she says.

One of the first parts of rehab was learning to sit up again.

"With a spinal injury your blood pressure gets really lowered. So I couldn't sit up in a wheelchair for longer than about five minutes without feeling faint," says Cresswell.

Then there were things like putting on socks or tying up her hair, although even by the time she left hospital she still could not do the latter while sitting up because she did not have any core strength or balance.

She remembers her timetable at the unit - official physio was 2pm til 3pm but she would be at the gym when it opened at 1pm, having also been at the physio room at 10am when that opened.

She was determined to keep busy - and creative about how to make that happen.

Take, for example, when she was told that it would take too many people to help her swim.

"Instead of saying anything, I just used to say OK, that's fine, but can I come and sit and watch? So, I was basically just making myself known by the swimming pool," says Cresswell, who credits her athlete's mindset for her drive and ability to take positives from every situation.

"So, I went for two weeks. I sat and watched these other people in the physios do swimming.

"And funnily enough, by the third week, they thought, 'we're going to have to let her go in the swimming pool now because she's just going to annoy us otherwise'."

It turned out, water was going to become a huge part of her life.

Around a week before she left the spinal unit, Cresswell attended the Spinal Games at Stoke Mandeville Hospital, which is for patients with spinal injuries who are either still in hospital or within a year post-accident, and is an opportunity to try different sports over four days.

"I got six out of six bull's eyes and won the archery out of 110 people," she says.

"It was a great stepping stone to coming home. And I think I kind of held on to that when I came home initially because the first while was really tough at home."

She left hospital on 8 October and by December had started wheelchair racing, going on to race 10Ks and a half-marathon, also doing wheelchair tennis and basketball.

"I was worried I would never find a sport that I wanted to put my whole energy into," she says. "I think I knew that horses were my hobby that got to turn into my sport and my career and lifestyle so I didn't know if that would be possible to find something like that."

Cresswell had got chatting to Olympic canoe athlete Deborah Kerr at an event run by the Women's Sport Trust charity who had told her to "have a go".

So, on 23 December last year, she did. Winter was "not the time to start a water sport" and she was "not a natural".

"My coach was too scared to let me off the bank in case I capsized," she laughs. "And that probably stayed, I don't think I left the bank for about a month."

A one-off taster session turned into twice a week and then eventually five times a week on the water. Four-hour training sessions, plus gym work three days a week.

One of the biggest challenges has been staying upright.

"I don't have any feedback of any part of my body if I am losing balance," she explains. "So I'm strapped into a seat because I've got no core function, but I can't actually feel that seat. So I basically feel like I'm floating.

"So my only thing I've got to know if I've lost balance is my head and my eyes. So that took a while to start to hone in and they always say, deaf people hear better than anybody else, don't they? And I think it's a bit the same.

"It's like, I've now tuned into how to balance myself without the use of the rest of my body. But I'd say the balance aspect is a big part of it alongside the technical, constant skill-based stuff that needs to be improved."

It is the technical aspect that she thinks has similarities to equestrian and which is why she thinks she enjoys it so much.

Her progress has been rapid, by anyone's standards. Not least her own.

"World Championships was definitely not the plan. It was a quiet goal after a while that if I could get the time, I might be able to go," says Cresswell, who alongside training is also doing media work.

"The time I needed to achieve was, I think, one minute 26 seconds. And anyway, I'm now down to one minute 18. So I've kind of over-achieved on that one, which has just been through repetition, practise, finding new ways to do things."

She has been selected to represent Great Britain at this month's Canoe Sprint and Para-Canoe World Championships in Poznan, Poland.

Having only ever raced once before in the UK her aims are modest.

"Honestly, stay up and get through the start and finish line," she says, explaining that she capsized before the start of a race she was due to do in April.

It is more about getting an international classification - which involves a series of medical tests to assess an athlete's impairment and demonstrating how much of your body you can use when paddling - so that she can be eligible to earn points at events that can lead to qualification for the 2028 Paralympics in Los Angeles.

Could she have pictured this when she was in hospital?

"I certainly wouldn't have imagined I was going to do para-canoe - I didn't even know [that] was a sport when I was in hospital," says Cresswell, who will compete in the VL1 (a canoe with a support float) and KL1 (kayak).

"But to be honest, I think what actually is more kind of crazy in my head is I couldn't even imagine January me doing this."

articles.title: Duke Champion Kyle Singler Calls Out Coach K in Alarming Videos
articles.summary: Former Duke star Kyle Singler named Coach K directly in three concerning videos, accusing his former coach of setting him up while pleading for help. The pos...
articles.body:
Former Duke star Kyle Singler directly accused Mike Krzyzewski of mistreating him and repeatedly pleaded with his former coach for help across three concerning new social media videos.

"Coach K has set me up," Singler says in one of the videos. "Set me up, man."

Singler, the Most Outstanding Player of Duke's 2010 national championship run under Krzyzewski, makes a series of serious and sometimes difficult-to-follow allegations throughout the clips. He claims people have broken into his home, taken money and compromised his accounts, while repeatedly saying he feels unable to leave his residence.

The videos provide no evidence establishing those allegations as fact.

What they do make clear is whom Singler wants to hear his message.

"Coach, where you at?" Singler says. "Help my brother out. Thought we on the same team, man."

Singler's first video is centered largely on Krzyzewski, who coached him for all four of his seasons at Duke.

"I have no power. I have no house," Singler says. "I've reached out to coach and everybody has turned the other way."

Singler then alleges that his power has been cut off and that people have broken into his house, stolen money and ruined his life.

"Reached out to Coach K," Singler says. "And all he did is sit me on the bench."

It isn't clear what Singler means by being put on the bench. Krzyzewski retired from coaching Duke following the 2021-22 season, more than a decade after Singler's college career ended.

Neither Krzyzewski nor Duke appears to have publicly responded to Singler's latest statements.

Singler Also Makes Accusation Involving Duke

The second video contains another direct appeal to his former coach and expands Singler's claims to Duke.

Singler says he has experienced confrontations while living in Oklahoma and claims he feels unable to leave his home.

"Coach, I need your help," he says. "Help, man. I'm stuck at my house and I can't leave. I feel imprisoned."

Singler later says his "life's on the line" and alleges that people are breaking into his home and accounts and taking money.

"Duke's all about it," Singler says. "I got Duke again begging for my money. Everybody's after my money, trying to kill me."

Those are Singler's allegations, and the videos do not establish that Duke, Krzyzewski or anyone affiliated with the university has engaged in the conduct he describes.

Singler concludes by again speaking directly to his former coach.

"Coach, you got again former player being mistreated and abused and you ain't doing nothing, man," he says. "Help out."

Third Video Continues Singler's Plea for Help

Singler continues the theme in a third clip, saying that his accounts are "hijacked and frozen" and claiming that people are watching his residence.

He again turns to the coach he addressed throughout the other videos.

"I need your help," Singler says. "I'm locked in my house and I have no freedom anymore."

Near the end, Singler says he has attempted to contact his former coach "many times" and accuses him of being "deflective" and leaving people behind.

"So, you got a player that's been traded, baby," Singler says.

It is unclear what Singler means by that remark. His professional basketball career ended years ago.

The new posts arrive after previous videos from Singler generated widespread concern within basketball.

In November 2024, Singler posted a video saying he had been mistreated and that he feared for his life. The Associated Press reported that the National Basketball Players Association subsequently contacted his family. Kevin Love, Isaiah Thomas and Andre Drummond were among the current and former NBA players who publicly offered support.

"I love you Kyle. Hit me whenever. Please," Love wrote at the time, according to the AP.

Singler later encountered legal trouble in Oklahoma. In October 2025, he was charged with one misdemeanor count of assault and battery in the presence of a child after an alleged incident involving his girlfriend, according to the Associated Press. Singler was released on bond after his arrest, the AP reported.

The latest three videos put his relationship with Duke back at the center of the story.

Singler wasn't a peripheral player under Krzyzewski. He spent four seasons at Duke, helped deliver the 2010 national championship and was named the tournament's Most Outstanding Player.

That history makes his repeated appeals particularly striking now.

Across all three videos, amidst a collection of allegations and grievances, Singler repeatedly comes back to one request directed at the coach with whom he won college basketball's biggest prize:

World No 1 women's player Aryna Sabalenka and 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic were the top seeds but lost in the first round, with the all-American pairing of Jessica Pegula and Taylor Fritz the second seeds.

articles.title: Fire in Pakistan hospital nursery kills at least 14 newborns, officials say
articles.summary: A fire at a nursery in a major government hospital in Pakistan's capital killed 14 newborns, hospital officials and the government said.
articles.body:
Islamabad — A fire at a nursery in a major government hospital in Pakistan's capital killed 14 newborns, hospital officials and the government said.

The nursery at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences housed 15 newborns when the fire broke out, hospital officials said. At least one baby was rescued.

Rescue officials said the fire began at about 6:45 a.m., apparently after the compressor of an air-conditioning unit exploded inside the nursery, which is part of the hospital's gynecology ward.

Firefighters quickly responded and extinguished the blaze, and rescue teams were carrying out cooling operations at the site, local media reported.

The ward was cordoned off and ambulances were seen outside the hospital building, a witness told the Reuters news service.

A hospital spokesperson didn't immediately respond to calls from The Associated Press seeking comment.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and ordered an immediate investigation. A statement from his office confirmed that 14 newborns had died.

"A tragedy involving children is an irreparable loss," Sharif said.

"The circumstances that led to the incident should be thoroughly reviewed, those responsible should be identified, and the strictest possible action should be taken," he added, according to French news agency AFP.

articles.title: Bristol Water issues first hosepipe ban in decades
articles.summary: Bristol Water says it must protect the River Severn, with the West Country in drought.
articles.body:
A water company has announced its first hosepipe ban caused by drought in more than 50 years, following the lead of other suppliers across the West.

Bristol Water says its "temporary restriction", will come into force from 00:01 BST on Thursday 27 August, to protect water resources in the River Severn.

Wessex Water, Thames Water and South West Water have already introduced bans this summer, with the South West formally declared as being in drought earlier this month.

"Introducing a hosepipe ban is never a decision we take lightly, and we fully appreciate the inconvenience it will cause," said Richard Stanbrook, director for drinking water services at Bristol Water.

This marks the first hosepipe ban in the Bristol Water area caused by drought since 1975, when a dry summer was then followed by 16 months of low rainfall.

However Bristol Water also introduced a short ban in 1990 because of a hole in the bottom of the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal, which then collapsed.

In a statement announcing the latest ban, Bristol Water said although the restriction did not come into force until Thursday, people were being asked to follow the ban immediately.

It includes not using hosepipes for watering gardens, washing cars, patios or boats or filling swimming and paddling pools.

When the weather is as dry as it has been this summer, Bristol Water takes more than half of its supply from river sources, including the Severn via the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal.

However, the Environment Agency and Natural Resources Wales have now applied a drought order to protect the river.

Bristol Water has also pointed to warnings around El Niño, a powerful natural climate phenomenon which pushes up global temperatures and could increase the risks of extreme weather.

Stanbrook said: "After an extended period of exceptionally low rainfall, combined with sustained high demand during the warmer weather, our region's rivers are under significant pressure.

"This is reflected in the Environment Agency's decision to apply for a drought order on the River Severn, where we take a proportion of our water during the summer months.

"The water resources we depend on, particularly the River Severn, support the wildlife, habitats and species that rely on water directly or indirectly, and it's critical we all carefully balance public water use with water needed for our natural environment to thrive.

"We take our responsibility for preserving the water environment very seriously and we know our customers do too. With next year predicted to be the warmest year on record, and with the added pressures from El Niño, we must all think about how we can protect the environment for future years, as well as today."

articles.title: In 1906, Quaker industrialist William Bancroft began buying land outside Wilmington to keep it open for the public; more than a century later, 1,359 acres became the largest unit of First State National Historical Park
articles.summary: US News: In 1906, industrialist William Poole Bancroft began buying land in Delawareâs Brandywine Valley to hold it in reserve for the health and well-being of.
articles.body: In 1906, industrialist William Poole Bancroft began buying land in Delawareâs Brandywine Valley to hold it in reserve for the health and well-being of the public. More than a century later, 1,359 acres of that land became the largest unit of First State National Historical Park.The story of the land, however, began much earlier. National Park service says the Brandywine Valley was originally home to the Lenape people, including the seasonal village of Queonemysing. The village was used for fishing and remained relatively undisturbed while Swedish and Dutch traders focused on the larger waterways in the area.That changed as English colonists, many of them Quakers, began moving further into the interior. Their arrival brought major changes to the valley and affected the Lenape community that had lived there. Over time, European settlement expanded into the area, changing how the land was used and occupied.By the early 18th century, Quaker immigrants had established farms and mills along the creeks. The waterways were important because they provided irrigation for fields, power for mills and routes for transportation. As settlement expanded away from the creek banks, farmers cleared more land and built stone farmhouses.The valley later developed a strong agricultural and industrial character. By the mid-19th century, farmers were cultivating much of the best agricultural land. The area also produced wool, finished cloth, paper and clover seeds. But the water-powered mills that had once played an important role gradually became outdated in the second half of the 19th century.Bancroft begins buying landBy the early 20th century, many of the mills along the Brandywine Creek had stopped operating and fallen into ruin. It was during this period that Bancroft began purchasing property in the valley.Bancroft was an heir to the Bancroft textile mills on the Brandywine. Starting in 1906, he bought land from farmers and small-scale industrialists. His stated purpose was to hold the properties in reserve for the health and well-being of the public.Bancroft eventually acquired more than 1,300 acres. About 1,100 of those acres would later become part of the Brandywine Valley tract of First State National Historical Park.His efforts were not limited to simply buying land. In 1919, he formed the Woodlawn Company. The organisation was later renamed Woodlawn Trustees Inc. Its aims included creating affordable housing and acquiring land for parkland and open space.The land remained privately owned but served as a park for many years. That eventually changed when part of it was transferred to the National Park Service.In 2013, roughly 1,105 acres were donated to the National Park Service. Another 254 acres were donated in 2021. Together, these donations brought the Brandywine Valley unit to 1,359 acres, making it the largest unit of First State National Historical Park.Land becomes national ParkThe land had already been used for recreation before it became part of the National Park Service. In 1959, the Woodlawn Trustees began building bridle paths so their officers and guests could explore more of the area.Some of the paths used existing farm roads, while others were newly created for recreation. By 1968, the paths had been opened to the public. People could use them for hiking, biking and horseback riding.The recreational use of the land has continued under the National Park Service. The Brandywine Valley unit now covers 1,359 acres along the border of Delaware and Pennsylvania.In 2024, the National Park Service completed a Comprehensive Trail Plan for the area. The plan sets out a designated shared-use trail network covering 27.8 miles. The plan includes rerouting, repairing and modifying trails in different parts of the Brandywine Valley unit.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

Pastor added further insurance with his second goal of the game.

Freshman Layla Haynes erupted for four goals to push the Rovers' unbeaten streak to three games. Josie App, Paisley Day and Elliott Smallfield added a goal apiece for Rootstown (2-1-1, 1-0-0 CVC) while Sammy Smolk and Charlie Wilson each tallied an assist.

The Vikings fell despite two goals from Alexis Henry and two assists from Koralee Jenior. Abigail Roberts had six saves for Waterloo (1-2-0, 0-1-0 Mahoning Valley Athletic Conference), which actually led in both corner kicks (4-2) and shots on goal (15-10).
